Title: Enhancing Domain-Specific English-Chinese Neural Machine Translation with Data Augmentation and Term Adaptation Techniques
Abstract: Neural Machine Translation (NMT) has achieved remarkable progress in natural language processing. However, developing domain-specific translation models with limited data remains a critical challenge, as NMT heavily relies on largescale datasets. This paper presents an English-Chinese NMT engine designed to address these challenges by leveraging domain adaptation, data augmentation, and innovative term translation techniques. The engine incorporates a placeholderbased fuzzy matching method and a model learning guidance strategy to enhance translation quality. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed engine significantly outperforms commercial systems in translating domain-specific content, particularly in the social media context. This work contributes to improving NMT for low-resource domains and highlights strategies for creating effective, adaptable translation models for specialized applications.

Title: Neural Machine Translation for Punjabi-English language pair using word-based tokenization
Abstract: Machine Translation (MT) is becoming essential for communication, and Neural Machine Translation (NMT) is currently considered the most effective approach for language translation. However, limited research has been conducted on translation for low-resource Indian languages. Languages like Punjabi which are highly complex in terms of morphology and pose significant challenges during translation. As the usage of Indian language, especially Punjabi continue to grow, the requirement for its higher quality translation is increasing. The Transformer architecture based models have shown promising results in various NLP tasks for such low-resource languages. This paper proposes NMT based approach for Punjabi-English (PA-EN) and English-Punjabi (EN-PA) pair using the transformer architecture with word-based tokenization. The proposed work has been evaluated using publicly available Samanantar dataset. It outperforms the state-of-the-art by 3.5% for PA-EN and 3.64% for EN-PA as measured using BLEU score.

Title: Optimization of Multilingual English Translation Model Based on Transformer Architecture and Transfer Learning Algorithm
Abstract: Traditional machine translation methods face problems such as low translation quality and limited model generalization ability. This study is based on the Transformer architecture and introduces a multi-head self-attention mechanism to capture the long-distance dependencies of words in a sentence. In the model training stage, a combination of unsupervised pre-training and supervised fine-tuning is used to learn the representation and mapping relationship of the input sequence. During the training process, the difference between the predicted output and the true label is calculated, and the model weights are updated through the back-propagation algorithm. The average BLEU score of the model on 15 translation tasks reached 90.2, which is 22.1% higher than the statistical machine translation method. At the same time, the highest translation time is only 61% of the statistical machine translation method, providing a new solution and technical path for low-resource language translation.

Title: Digitalizing Maguindanaon Language Using Corpus-Based Approach and Statistical Machine Translation (Smt)
Abstract: This paper focuses on Maguindanaon, a language spoken by the Maguindanaon people in the Philippines, particularly in the provinces of Maguindanao del Norte and del Sur. With about two million speakers, the language has significant cultural value but is facing a decline as younger generations shift to more widely spoken languages. Unfortunately, there are limited resources and digital tools available to support the language, putting its future at risk. To address this, this paper develops a small-scale Maguindanaon-English bilingual corpus and uses it to test Statistical Machine Translation (SMT) models, including IBM Models 1 and 2 and a Phrase-based model. The goal was to explore the potential for using machine translation to bridge the gap between Maguindanaon and English. Although the results showed that all models struggled due to the small size of the corpus, with the Phrase-based model achieving the highest but still low BLEU scores, the study highlights the potential of machine translation for under-resourced languages. The findings emphasize the need for a larger, better-aligned corpus and improved techniques to enhance translation quality, laying the groundwork for future efforts in both language preservation and machine translation for Maguindanaon.

Title: A Neural Network Approach for Speech to Text Translation of Low Resource Language
Abstract: Developing speech translation systems for low-resource languages remains a major issue because lack of annotated datasets and linguistic resources. This work introduces a neural speech-to-text translation framework designed for low-resource Indian languages, with Konkani as a case study. The proposed system converts spoken Konkani into English text through Hindi as a pivot language, integrating Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) and Neural Machine Translation (NMT) models within a unified architecture. The methodology involves audio preprocessing, feature extraction, and pivot-based translation using pretrained models such as IndicConformer and Transformer-based NMT to ensure fluency and adaptability. By leveraging transfer learning and multilingual modeling, the approach effectively addresses issues of data scarcity, accent variation, and linguistic diversity. In comparison, our proposed pipeline attains 29.6% WER and 28.1 BLEU, demonstrating competitive performance despite operating in a low-resource setting. These results show that our model performs on par with, and in some cases surpasses, existing benchmarks for similar multilingual pipelines.

Title: Maximizing Model Adaptation for Low-Resource Languages: A Progressive Unfreezing Strategy for Spanish-Aymara Translation
Abstract: Neural Machine Translation has revolutionized global communication for high-resource language pairs; however, indigenous languages such as Aymara remain underserved due to the scarcity of parallel corpora and computational resources. This work presents an adaptive progressive training approach to improve Meta’s NLLB-200 model for Spanish–Aymara translation quality. We constructed a parallel corpus of 35,009 sentence pairs primarily extracted from biblical content, implementing a progressive layer freezing and unfreezing training strategy. Our methodology increased the chrF++ metric from 32.93 to 55.88, demonstrating a substantial improvement over the baseline performance. Additionally, we developed a publicly accessible web interface to facilitate adoption by Spanish-Speakers and Aymara communities. This study demonstrates the feasibility of developing automatic translation systems for indigenous lowresource languages by combining a carefully constructed parallel corpus, an efficient fine-tuning strategy, and a publicly accessible deployment. Our results contribute to digital inclusion and the preservation of cultural heritage.

Title: Grammatical Error Correction in Slovak Using Neural Machine Translation and No Language Left Behind
Abstract: Grammatical error correction aims to identify and rectify linguistic inaccuracies in text, thereby enhancing communication and comprehension. This study investigates the ap-plication of neural machine translation techniques, particularly the No Language Left Behind technique for GEC in Slovak, a morphologically rich language. We constructed datasets containing deliberate grammatical errors and used them to train models capable of detecting and correcting these errors. By introducing random character and word-level transformations, we simulated realistic grammatical errors, creating a robust testing ground for model evaluation. Our experimental results demonstrate significant improvements in performance metrics such as BLEU score, Word Error Rate, and Sentence Error Rate. The findings highlight the potential of NMT-based approaches in developing efficient and accurate GEC systems for underrepresented languages.

Title: Real-Time on-Device Neural Machine Translation for Dynamic Multilingual Mobile Application Localization
Abstract: MobileNMT, a small on-device neural machine translation solution, dynamically localises static UI and APIfetched data in Android apps without strings.xml localisation files. With a quantised encoder-decoder Transformer architecture optimised for TFLite, MobileNMT achieves a compact model size (12.6 MB) and low inference latency ($\sim 90$- 100 ms) on mid-range mobile hardware. Shared embeddings and parameter-efficient compression configurations are key developments. Based on comprehensive tests, MobileNMT achieves a BLEU score of 24.9, maintains runtime memory below 50 MB, reduces APK size by 70%, allows offline operation, and protects user privacy. Scalability and performance are improved over static localisation files and important translation baselines like Google ML Kit (offline) and uncompressed Transformers. MobileNMT appears to be a flexible and stable option for multilingual mobile app development in dynamic, resource-constrained contexts.

Title: Exploring the Effect of Data Augmentation on Neural Machine Translation Between Indonesian and Madurese Languages Using the LSTM Model
Abstract: Neural Machine Translation (NMT) has shown significant potential in producing high-quality translations, particularly for well-resourced language pairs. The efficacy of NMT is significantly dependent on extensive parallel corpora, presenting a difficulty for languages with scarce linguistic resources. This study focuses on developing an NMT system to translate Indonesian to Madurese, leveraging the Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) architecture. LSTM is particularly well-suited for sequence-to-sequence learning tasks, as it effectively captures long-term dependencies in text data. To mitigate the challenges posed by limited datasets, this research employs data augmentation techniques to expand the training corpus. These methods enhance the diversity and volume of input data, allowing the model to learn linguistic patterns more effectively. The experimental results demonstrate that the LSTM-based NMT model achieves an average BLEU score of 53%, reflecting a significant step toward bridging the gap in machine translation for low-resource languages. This work highlights the potential of combining advanced machine learning techniques with innovative data strategies to support the preservation and accessibility of underrepresented languages, such as Madurese.

Title: Overview of Research on Low-Resource Language Machine Translation Based on Artificial Intelligence
Abstract: This study examines the role of artificial intelligence in low-resource language translation, focusing on preserving endangered languages and cultural heritage. It reviews foundational Neural Machine Translation (NMT) theories, evaluates advancements in key technologies like data augmentation and transfer learning, and assesses their impact on translation quality. Given the scarcity of machine translation methods for low-resource languages, the paper reviews current research in multimodal, paragraph-level, and multilingual machine translation, offering insights for future studies. Case studies are included to demonstrate these technologies' practical applications and challenges. Finally, the paper explores opportunities and challenges NMT models face in low-resource contexts, aiming to enhance translation quality and support cultural heritage preservation.

Title: Fine Tuning the BART Model for Mon-English Neural Machine Translation
Abstract: Fine-tuning large pre-trained models has been proven successful for many tasks in NLP. This paper describes the procedures for adapting the target language neural machine translation (NMT) for Mon-English using BART (Bidirectional and Auto-Regressive Transformers) model fine-tuning. The goal of this paper has been translated Mon, which is considered to be a lesser-resourced language, to English fine tuning with BART model. This paper analyzes the performance of the BART model while employing it in machine translation from Mon to English on a parallel corpus of 25k parallel sentences. There are two ways of preparing the Mon language. First, the Mon text was tokenized using a mon vocabulary mapping whereas the English text used the BART tokenizer. This setting has attained a BLEU score of 30.14, which reflects moderate translation quality. In the second approach, the Mon text was tokenized using a SentencePiece-based Byte Pair Encoding (BPE) model and the English text still used the BART tokenizer. This resulted in significantly higher translation performance, with a BLEU score of 38.72, proving that the application of SentencePiece BPE in tokenizing Mon text combined with the BART tokenizer for English was successful. These results show that the choice of tokenization method for the source language has an essential role in improving machine translation performance for low-resource languages like Mon.

Title: Computational Approaches to Neural Machine Translation in Low-Resource Languages: A Bibliometric Review (2017–July 2025)
Abstract: While recent advances in neural machine translation (NMT) have revolutionized communication for major languages, a critical research-practice gap persists for the world’ s 3,000+ low-resource languages (LRLs), which remain marginalized due to algorithmic biases toward high-resource paradigms and chronic data scarcity. This bibliometric review interrogates 188 publications (2017 – July 2025) to map the evolution of LRL-NMT, revealing three unresolved tensions: Architectural lock-in, where Transformer dominance (48.2% keyword frequency) suppresses innovation for morphologically diverse LRLs despite 38.7% CAGR growth; data-model divergence, as persistent challenges in morpheme segmentation (22.7%) and unknown word handling (19.1%) outpace computational solutions; and geographic fragmentation, with India (28.7%) and China (32.1%) producing 60.8% of institutional output while Global South regions face systemic exclusion (<6% contribution). Crucially, deployment governance gaps (9.6% keyword prevalence) remain unaddressed by current cross-lingual transfer strategies. We contend that equitable progress necessitates dismantling these asymmetries through decentralized corpora development and adaptive architectural frameworks.

Title: Enhancing Cebuano-English Neural Machine Translation Using Pseudo-Labeling and Transformer Architectures
Abstract: This paper presents a semi-supervised neural machine translation (NMT) pipeline that significantly improves Cebuano $\leftrightarrow$ English translation quality. Our approach achieved a 24.3-point improvement in BLEU score, increasing from 60.89 to 85.19, while maintaining fluency and semantic adequacy. Starting with a 0.46-million-sentence parallel corpus, we forward-translated 2.4 million monolingual English sentences into Cebuano using a pseudo-labeling method. These outputs were filtered using confidence scores and length ratios, then combined with gold-standard data to retrain a Transformer-based MarianMT model. The final system preserved structural fidelity and semantic accuracy while delivering substantial gains in translation quality. Experiments revealed that (i) a curriculum beginning with 70 % pseudo-labeled and 30 % gold-standard data yields the fastest convergence, and (ii) attention maps remain linguistically coherent despite the inclusion of synthetic data. These findings demonstrate that pseudo-labeling is a cost-effective and scalable strategy for low-resource Philippine languages.

Title: Neural Machine Translation in Low-Resourced Languages: Case of Dholuo-Swahili Translation
Abstract: This study developed a Neural Machine Translation (NMT) model for Dholuo-Swahili translation, addressing the lack of translation resources for lowresource languages in Kenya. Using the OpenNMT-py framework, the model was trained on a parallel dataset of 27,415 sentence pairs from two datasets to improve model performance. Performance was evaluated using BLEU (Bilingual Evaluation Understudy), METEOR (Metric for Evaluation of Translation with Explicit Ordering), perplexity (PPL), and prediction scores, with results showing a BLEU score of 16.29, METEOR score of 0.27, and PPL of 1.88, indicating moderate translation accuracy. Despite achieving low PPL, fluency and lexical accuracy challenges persisted due to limited training data and linguistic differences. Future research will focus on expanding datasets, leveraging multilingual models like LLaMA 3.2, and integrating hybrid approaches to improve translation quality. This work contributes to digital inclusion, language preservation, and enhanced crosslinguistic communication for underrepresented languages in Kenya.

Title: Multilingual Parameter-Sharing Adapters: A Method for Optimizing Low-Resource Neural Machine Translation
Abstract: Adapter-based Multilingual Neural Machine Translation (MNMT) has become a significant approach in low-resource language translation by mitigating data imbalances between high-resource and low-resource language pairs and reducing training costs. However, existing adapter-based methods lack generalization in cross-lingual settings, particularly under low-resource conditions, where their scalability is limited. Additionally, current methods often introduce independent adapter modules for each language, leading to a linear increase in model parameters with the number of languages. To address these challenges, we propose a multilingual parameter-sharing adapter approach. Moreover, we introduce a neural architecture search (NAS)-based strategy to improve translation performance. Experimental results demonstrate that the multilingual parameter-sharing adapter exhibits competitive performance on both low-resource and high-resource datasets. The multilingual parameter-sharing adapter method has only 400K trainable parameters, which is 20× lower than the parameters of the traditional adapter method.

Title: A Knowledge Distillation Based Translation Prompt Information Fusion Method for Neural Machine Translation
Abstract: Autoregressive (AR) models represented by Transformer has attained the highest performance benchmarks in neural machine translation, which benefits from the powerful learning ability of the model with the attention mechanism. It differs from the way human translators translate a sentence, where prior knowledge plays a important role. Inspired by this, a knowledge distillation based translation prompt information fusion method is proposed to improve the AR model. It introduces two modules to improve the AR model: translation prompt information fusion and knowledge distillation. The main steps can be summarized as follows: Firstly, Training a non-autoregressive (NAR) model based on the bilingual corpus. Then, the translation prompt information generated by NAR are integrated into the AR model from two aspects. On the on hand, incorporating the translation produced by the NAR model into the decoder of the AR model. On the other hand, utilizing the output distribution of the NAR model to guide the output distribution of the AR model. Experimental results across several translation tasks with low-resource and rich-resource indicate the effectiveness of the proposed method.

Title: A Context-Aware Framework for Reducing Offensive Language into Polite Equivalents in English-to-Tamil Neural Machine Translation
Abstract: In neural machine translation (NMT), it is crucial to effectively handle offensive or slur words; particularly in low-resource languages like Tamil, it is all the more important to translate English words and phrases and present them in a cultural and respectful manner. In the proposed approach, the use of a context-aware NMT framework detects and translates offensive English phrases and expensive English phrases and expressions into a dignified and polite manner. The conversion includes a combination of politeness-based on dictionary mapping and transformer-based paraphrasing. The accuracy of this approach is 95.4 %, and the quality, BLEU score, is 78.2. The presence of a confidence scoring mechanism produces accurate and reliable translations. The proposed approach applies well in moderation requirements for social media. Furthermore, the same approach can be used for AI-based customer support and content filtering. In low-resource languages like Tamil, the management and control of offensive languages and expressions is of utmost importance to achieve acceptable and respectful translations.)

Title: Quantifying the Impact of Data Scale and Quality on Neural Machine Translation for Low-Resource Language Pair
Abstract: This paper analyzes a Transformer Architecture model for Manipuri-English machine translation, focusing on data quality and size. Title: Advancing Neural Machine Translation for Under-Resourced Indic Languages: Manipuri and Sindhi
Abstract: Although the availability of digital content in English has grown exponentially, accessibility is still in short supply for under-resourced languages. Machine translation (MT) offer a crucial solution for bridging the language gap. Recent advancements in Neural Machine Translation (NMT), especially transformer-based approaches, have significantly improved MT. This study proposes the use of a specialized Dense Transformer model for MT between under-resourced English and Manipuri (Meetei script) languages, as well as between English and Sindhi (Devanagari script) languages. In contrast to conventional methods that rely on large-scale pre-trained models, our proposed model is trained end-to-end on the English-Manipuri and English-Sindhi datasets and assessed against IndicTrans2, a multilingual NMT, using BPCC training data, IN22 test sets, and the FLORES-22 validation set. Furthermore, we incorporate the IndicTransToolkit preprocessing pipeline into our proposed Dense Transformer process and run experiments with and without this incorporation. Results indicate that preprocessing improves the translation accuracy, particularly for English→Indic languages, with significant improvements in chrF++ and overall translation quality. Although IndicTrans2 still has an edge in Indic→English translation, our proposed Dense Transformer models exhibit more robust performance in English→Indic tasks, especially for IN22-Conv and IN22-Gen datasets. Title: Hindi-English Machine Translation: A Comprehensive Comparative Analysis of Paradigms and Systems
Abstract: The demand for accurate Hindi-to-English machine translation (MT) is growing due to India’s digital expansion and the global prominence of English. This paper presents a comprehensive comparative analysis of the evolution of MT systems for this language pair, from early rule-based approaches to modern neural paradigms. We evaluate seminal and contemporary systems—including Anglabharti, Anubharti, Google Translate, and Sampark—against a multi-faceted framework assessing linguistic accuracy, fluency, contextual adequacy, and computational efficiency. Our findings indicate that while Neural Machine Translation (NMT) sets a new benchmark in fluency, hybrid models that integrate linguistic knowledge with data-driven approaches remain crucial for handling the morphological richness and semantic nuances of Hindi. The analysis concludes that the future of Hindi-English MT lies in hybrid architectures and ontology-driven models, especially for low-resource and domain-specific scenarios.

Title: A Decoder-Only Generative Framework for Low-Resource English-Telugu Neural Machine Translation
Abstract: The paper deals with the problem of English-Telugu neural machine translation (NMT) in the conditions of extremely low resources. Telugu is a morphologically rich, free word order, Dravidian language that poses serious challenges to standard encoder-decoder NMT systems that are highly dependent on large parallel corpora and computational resources. To address these issues, a new decoder-only generative model was created, which is trained on the GPT-2 transformer model, but with bilingual English-Telugu translation in mind. The methodology uses resource-efficient fine-tuning techniques, such as sparse parallel data augmentation with synthetic data, semantic filtering with the Universal Sentence Encoder, and preprocessing techniques, such as subword tokenization. The model was tested using several metrics, such as BLEU, ROUGE, and cosine similarity, on standard datasets, such as FLORES-101, and it was found that the model can produce lexically correct, semantically consistent, and structurally faithful translations. The solution proposed fills the gap between the resource limitations and quality of translation by removing redundant model elements and concentrating on sentence-level fidelity. The study contributes to the research on low-resource language translation, providing practical information and a scalable architecture to similar language pairs that face the problem of data scarcity.

Title: A Keyword Exchange-Based Data Augmentation Method for Low-Resource Neural Machine Translation
Abstract: Recent advancements in Transformer-based architectures have established new benchmarks in neural machine translation (NMT), though their efficacy remains constrained by the availability of large-scale parallel corpora. This limitation becomes particularly pronounced for low-resource language pairs, where the scarcity of bilingual training data often leads to suboptimal translation performance. To address this challenge, we introduce Keyword Exchange (KE), a novel data augmentation framework designed to enhance translation quality in data-scarce scenarios. The proposed methodology operates through a three-stage pipeline: (1) A selective filtering approach is first applied to identify and retain high-quality sentence pairs from both source and target language corpora; (2) The KE algorithm is then deployed on the filtered target-side sentences, strategically substituting keywords to generate syntactically valid yet semantically divergent pseudo-monolingual data; (3) Finally, an Alignment Mixture strategy synthesizes these augmented monolingual fragments with their corresponding source-side counterparts, producing a robust pseudo-parallel corpus that significantly expands the effective training set. Empirical validation across multiple low-resource translation benchmarks demonstrates the framework's superiority over conventional baselines. Notably, our approach achieves a maximum BLEU score improvement of 0.74 points compared to a strong Transformer-based baseline, outperforming several state-of-the-art data augmentation techniques.

Title: An Adaptive Multilingual and Morphology-Aware Framework for Low-Resource Indian Language Translation
Abstract: In recent years, Neural Machine Translation (NMT) has gained importance for enabling cross-lingual communication, yet low-resource Indian languages continue to face difficulties owing to limited corpora and complex morphology. However, a recent study on Kannada-Tulu translation introduced a Transformer-based NMT model with part-of-speech (POS) tagging, but it was constrained by a very small dataset and achieved only modest performance improvements. Therefore, Adaptive Multilingual Morphology-Aware Neural Machine Translation (AMM-NMT) was proposed. Initially, data are collected from the newly released English-Tulu parallel corpus and large-scale Samanantar corpus of Indic language datasets. Then, the data undergoes cleaning, normalization, and back-translation to enrich scarce Tulu resources, followed by Sentence-Piece subword tokenization to handle vocabulary diversity. Furthermore, training was performed using multilingual pre-training on related Dravidian pairs from Samanantar. Furthermore, fine-tuning of English-Tulu was enhanced through curriculum learning and adapter layers for adaptive transfer. Finally, the model integrates morphological feature embeddings (POS, case, tense, number, and gender) to capture linguistic richness, enabling the generation of fluent Tulu translations from Kannada or English inputs. Experimental results show that the proposed AMM-NMT achieves a Bilingual Evaluation Understudy (BLEU) score of 27.3, character n-gram F-score (chrF) of 41.6%, and Word Error Rate (WER) of 42.1%.

Title: Lite Mongolian-Chinese Neural Machine Translation: Dynamic Convolution with Long-Range Attention
Abstract: Neural Machine Translation (NMT) has achieved significant progress for high-resource language pairs but still faces challenges with low-resource pairs like Mongolian-Chinese. Mongolian presents unique grammatical and semantic modeling difficulties as an agglutinative language with rich morphology and SOV word order (Subject-Object-Verb). Taking Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) and Transformers as examples: CNNs struggle to capture long-range dependencies, while Transformers, despite their global modeling capabilities, impose high computational costs. Existing Mongolian-Chinese NMT methods often prioritize translation quality but overlook computational efficiency, limiting their applicability on resource-constrained devices. This paper proposes a lightweight model, Dynamic Convolution with Long-Range Attention (DCLA), which balances translation quality and efficiency. DCLA uses a recognizer module to analyze Mongolian-specific features, such as sentence length, structural complexity, and low-frequency word distribution. It effectively addresses syntactic challenges caused by SOV-SVO word order differences and semantic difficulties posed by polysemous and low-frequency words. DCLA adopts two strategies based on sample complexity: applying convolution for simpler samples to reduce computational cost and multi-head attention for complex samples to enhance modeling. Experiments demonstrate that DCLA outperforms the state-of-the-art Transformer model in Mongolian-Chinese translation, with a 2.7-point BLEU improvement, a 21% reduction in parameters, and a 40% decrease in computational cost.

Title: Linguistic and Computational Solutions for Translating Lexical Lacunae in Neural Machine Translation Systems
Abstract: In recent years, the exponential growth of neural machine translation (NMT) systems has led to significant improvements in automated multilingual communication. However, these systems still struggle with the accurate and contextually appropriate translation of lexical lacunae—words or expressions that are deeply embedded in one culture and have no direct equivalents in another. This research proposes a hybrid methodology that combines linguistic classification, ontology-based semantic mapping, and Transformer-based NMT adaptation to enhance the translation of culturally and conceptually bound lexical gaps. A total of 182 lacunae expressions were identified across Uzbek-English and Turkish-English corpora and categorized into three main types: cultural, administrative-legal, and lexical-conceptual lacunae. These were encoded in a domain-specific bilingual ontology, which provided semantic descriptors and translation strategies. The ontology was integrated into the NLLB-200 neural translation framework via a lacunae-detection and input-enrichment module. Experimental results demonstrated a significant improvement in translation quality. The enhanced model achieved BLEU score gains of +6.3 for Uzbek-English and +4.7 for Turkish-English translation tasks, and a 43% increase in lacunae-aware adequacy score (LAAS). Qualitative analysis confirmed that the enriched translations better preserved cultural and semantic integrity. The findings indicate that combining linguistic insights with machine learning techniques can address one of the key limitations in current translation technologies and offer scalable solutions for low-resource languages.

Title: Adaptive k-Nearest-Neighbor Machine Translation with Domain Relevance for Chinese-Mongolian Husbandry Domain
Abstract: Currently, there is a significant lack of Mongolian translation resources for technical exchanges in the husbandry industry. To validate our proposed method, we collected Chinese corpora related to the husbandry industry and constructed parallel Chinese-Mongolian husbandry corpora through manual translation. Experimental results demonstrate that our method achieved improvements of 4.67 BLEU points and 3.52 BLEU points compared to the kNN-NMT and Adaptive kNN-MT methods, respectively.

Title: Enhancing Neural Machine Translation from Spanish-Zapoteco by Fine-Tuning Transformer Models
Abstract: Zapoteco is an Indigenous language spoken in southern Mexico, primarily in Oaxaca, where regional variants exist. Although the language is still in use, the dominance of Spanish poses a threat to its survival. To help preserve Zapoteco culture, technological strategies are being explored, particularly through Natural Language Processing (NLP) models for translation. These tools aim to assist Zapoteco speakers who are literate in their native language but have limited Spanish proficiency. This study evaluates three machine translation models—mBART, MarianMT, and M2M100—for adapting to Zapoteco, leveraging synthetic sentences inspired by rural community language due to the lack of digital resources. Results indicated that mBART provided the best translations, followed by M2M100, while MarianMT struggled with contextualization. The research demonstrates that innovative approaches like synthetic data can improve translation for underdocumented Indigenous languages.

Title: Utilizing Morpheme-Based Translation Units to Enhance Bidirectional Amharic-Khimtagne Machine Translation with Deep Learning
Abstract: Neural Machine Translation (NMT), a critical application of NLP, automates translation between natural languages without human interaction. This research develops a bidirectional machine translation system for Amharic and Khimtagne, two morphologically rich Ethiopian languages. Building a translation model for this pair improves digital inclusion, information access, and helps preserve indigenous languages. We created a parallel corpus of 17,153 aligned sentence pairs from religious literature, educational resources, news, and official documents. Both word-based and morpheme-based segmentation strategies were used, with Morfessor for unsupervised morphological analysis. The dataset was tested with deep learning models, including LSTM, LSTM with Attention, CNN with Attention, and Transformer, in both directions: Amharic–Khimtagne and Khimtagne–Amharic. The Transformer model based on morphemes performed best, with BLEU scores of 22.99 for Khimtagne-to-Amharic and 23.42 for Amharic-to-Khimtagne. Compared to word-based methods, these results show morpheme-level units handle the intricate morphology of both languages, increasing accuracy. The study acknowledges dataset size and subject diversity limits. Future research will expand the corpus and explore training methods to improve quality. This research advances NMT for under-resourced languages and supports inclusive AI in Ethiopia.

Title: Towards Better APE: Improving Neural Machine Translation for Under-Resourced Languages via Hybrid-Attention Dual-Encoder Post Editing
Abstract: Automatic Post Editing (APE) is a crucial method focused on enhancing the quality of machine-translated text through learning from human post-edited pairs. Although research into APE has progressed for Machine Translation (MT) of numerous high-resource languages, it is rarely explored for under-resourced languages like Kannada, Tamil, and Malayalam. To bridge this gap, this paper presents a novel hybrid-attention dual-encoder model specifically designed for APE. The designed method is compared with the classical concatenation and crossattention mechanisms. The Kannada-Sanskrit (Kan-San) and Kannada-Tulu (Kan-Tul) language pairs are used as a case study to train APE models in both the directions. Results show that the hybrid-attention model produces better translation quality with Bilingual Evaluation Understudy (BLEU) scores of 14.80 and 36.58 for Sanskrit-Kannada (San-Kan) and Tulu-Kannada (Tul-Kan) language pairs, respectively.

Title: Hybrid Framework for Hinglish to English Machine Translation using Multi-lingual Transformers for Social Media Discourse
Abstract: In India, over 19,500 dialects with 121 major languages are spoken, making accurate communication challenging, thus highlighting the need for effective translation solutions. The existing machine translation systems are often inaccurate and face challenges due to limited or insufficient linguistic data and research for low-resource and code-mixed languages, such as Hinglish. To improve the translation of Hinglish low-resource language, to standard English, we propose a neural machine translation framework comprising four major steps: dataset acquisition, text normalization and pre-processing, translation using multi-lingual transformers, and performance evaluation. The experimentation is performed on two varying-size datasets representing social media discourse: Hinglish-TOP (10896 instances) and PHINC (13738 instances). The datasets are normalized, preprocessed, and passed to the proposed translation system. The translation system comprises Google Cloud Translation API (GAPI), mBART, and MarianMT multi-lingual transformers. The GAPI leverages Google’s pre-trained or translation-focused large language models (LLMs) to offer the scalability, ease of use, and cost-effectiveness of Google Cloud’s infrastructure. The quality of the translation is evaluated using recent evaluation metrics such as BLEU, METEOR, and WER scores. The proposed GAPI+mBART approach obtains better results than existing machine translation techniques/approaches, i.e., an average BLEU score of 0.342, an average METEOR score of 0.512, and 0.692 WER on the PHINC dataset. Also, the proposed GAPI+mBART approach performed better than the proposed GAPI+MarianMT approach on Hinglish-TOP datasets

Title: Hybrid Optimization Algorithm and Transformer Design for Low-Resource Chinese-African Neural Machine Translation
Abstract: With the continuous development of China Africa economic and trade relations, the demand for multilingual information transmission on translation tasks is also constantly increasing. Traditional translation methods have shortcomings in efficiency and accuracy, making it difficult to cope with complex economic and trade exchanges. This article proposes an algorithm architecture for intelligent management and optimization of multilingual resources based on a machine translation framework. It carries out cleaning, denoising, matching and other work at the data level to ensure resource quality; Enhance cross linguistic semantic modeling ability through neural network layers and fusion attention mechanisms; Realize self optimization iteration through deep neural networks and hybrid pattern structures. The experiment aimed to verify economic and trade texts, and the results showed a significant improvement in translation accuracy and efficiency. It can effectively solve the problem of multilingual corpus and achieve excellent application effects in practical translation, model stability, and application. It can provide technical and methodological support for cross-border e-commerce, contract translation, and government policy interpretation in China and Africa.

Title: Sarcasm-Aware Neural Translation for Informal Social Media Texts in Low-Resource Languages
Abstract: The performance of integrated social media translators remains inconsistent when dealing with texts that contain sarcasm. One contributing factor is the informal nature of language commonly used on these platforms, which often confuses standard translation models. This study explores the challenge of interpreting sarcasm in machine translation, with a particular focus on the Telugu language. We propose fine-tuned transformer-based models for two tasks: interpreting sarcasm within English texts and translating sarcastic English into accurate Telugu. We evaluate both direct and indirect approaches one translating sarcastic English directly into honest Telugu, and the other converting sarcastic English into honest English before translating into Telugu. Our methodology combines natural language processing techniques for both sarcasm interpretation and translation, addressing a gap in existing literature that often overlooks the need for sarcasm explanation. Furthermore, we highlight the essential role of human annotation in overcoming persistent challenges in open class neural machine translation, especially for underrepresented languages. This work aims to contribute to the development of more effective models for handling sarcasm and related complexities in low-resource language translation.

Title: Improving Speech Translation Through Data Augmentation with Data in Similar Languages
Abstract: Previous studies have shown that utilizing training data in similar languages can reduce translation errors in machine translation (MT). However, its potential in speech translation (ST) remains underexplored. In this study, we propose a novel method to enhance cross-modal training of ST models by incorporating external ST data from the same language group without explicit language tagging. We evaluate our method based on the ConST model on the CoVoST 2 Es-En dataset, and experimental results show that the performance improves as more ST data in similar languages is introduced. The model trained with 400 hours of external ST data in similar languages improved the BLEU score by 11.42% and 10.74% compared to the baseline model with no external data and the model trained with 1 million external Es-En MT data. These results demonstrate that our approach can improve ST performance, especially under low-resource conditions.

Title: English to Sanskrit Translation Using Sequence-to-Sequence with Attention
Abstract: Historical languages like Sanskrit require preservation for linguistic research and cultural heritage. English-to-Sanskrit translation remains challenging due to complex grammar and limited parallel data. This paper presents an English-to-Sanskrit translation system based on a Seq2Seq model with attention. The system achieves a validation accuracy of 99.60% and a BLEU score of 0.889, demonstrating substantial improvement over baseline methods. These results confirm that neural approaches provide reliable, fluent, and grammatically consistent translations for low-resource languages. Furthermore, the real-time translation interface demonstrates the system's practical utility. The findings indicate that modern AI can effectively support cultural preservation, bridge the gap between classical and contemporary language studies, and advance research in low-resource neural machine translation.

Title: A Transformer-Based Framework for Domain-Sensitive Amharic-English Neural Machine Translation With Character-Aware Subword Encoding
Abstract: An NMT framework that has been adapted to the domain of low-resourced and morphologically complex languages has been developed for translating from Amharic to English. Through the translation, domain adaptation and subword level segmentation pair and the results for the translated text confirms the Amharic to English translation underwent a boosted performance which speaks to the level of improvement of the translation model. This serves as a groundwork as an entry point for further research on new areas pertaining to the neural architectures of machine translations of Semitic and other languages of complicated morphology.

Title: Development of a Transfer Learning-Based NMT Framework using mBART and mT5 for Indonesian and Local Languages in Low-Resource Settings
Abstract: Indonesia has more than 700 local languages, yet most remain digitally underrepresented and lack parallel corpora for Natural Language Processing, limiting the development of machine translation systems and restricting digital access for local communities. This study addresses this gap by proposing a Neural Machine Translation framework for Indonesian and low-resource regional languages using transfer learning with mBART and mT5. The workflow includes corpus construction, sentence normalization, subword tokenization, data augmentation through back-translation, and standardized fine-tuning applied to both models. Experiments were conducted on Javanese, Sundanese, and Batak Toba under identical training and evaluation settings. Results demonstrate that transfer learning significantly improves translation performance compared to a baseline Transformer model, with mT5 achieving the highest BLEU, chrF, and human evaluation scores, producing translations that are more fluent and semantically aligned. The contributions of this research include a reproducible NMT framework, an Indonesian pivot-language strategy, a systematic model comparison, and a deployable prototype. Overall, the findings confirm multilingual transfer learning as an effective and scalable solution for advancing NMT in Indonesia’s low-resource languages and supporting long-term language preservation.

Title: Meranaw-English NMT: Corpus Construction and Transformer Fine-Tuning for Low-Resource Language Pair
Abstract: Neural Machine Translation (NMT) has made a great progress in high-resource languages, but low-resource languages like Meranaw are still underserved. This study bridges that gap by introducing METC-22K, the first MeranawEnglish Text Corpus with $\boldsymbol{\sim} \mathbf{2 2 K}$ sentence pairs. Data was sourced from dictionaries, religious texts, and everyday phrases, then thoroughly preprocessed and augmented. We then used this corpus to fine-tune two separate transformer models for translations in both directions. Automated evaluation got 0.62 BLEU for Meranaw → English and 0.33 for English → Meranaw. A native language expert also confirmed that 74% of the translations were grammatically correct and $\mathbf{6 5 \%}$ preserved the meaning. This work provides a valuable dataset and fine-tuning methods for NMT for underrepresented languages.

Title: Spanish-Mapudungun Translation using Transfer Learning for Low-resource Languages
Abstract: This work addresses Neural Machine Translation (NMT) for Spanish–Mapudungun, an endangered and digitally under-resourced indigenous language of South America with polysynthetic and agglutinative morphology. We explore transfer learning as a strategy to mitigate data scarcity, initializing Spanish–Mapudungun models from high-resource pairs (Spanish–English and Spanish–Finnish). Using a standardized 10,000-pair corpus, we show that transfer learning markedly improves translation quality in both directions over models trained from scratch. We further analyze whether the linguistic characteristics of the parent language—particularly morphological similarity—affect transfer effectiveness. Results indicate that both parent models achieve similar gains, suggesting that vocabulary coverage and tokenization dominate over morphological resemblance. These findings demonstrate the utility of transfer learning for endangered languages and underscore the need for linguistically informed methods and community involvement in revitalization efforts.

Title: Automated Medical Translation Device: Afrikaans to English with Disease Prediction
Abstract: This research presents an AI-powered device that enhances healthcare by providing medical translation from English to Afrikaans and disease prediction. Utilizing neural machine translation with an attention mechanism, the device facilitates communication between healthcare professionals and Afrikaans-speaking patients, especially in the under-resourced areas. The device also features a healthcare chatbot that uses decision tree classifiers and support vector machines (SVM) to diagnose diseases from user-reported symptoms. This integration aids in early disease detection and improves diagnostic accuracy, while the text-to-speech function and user-friendly interface ensure accessibility. Addressing both communication barriers and diagnostic needs, this technology aims to make healthcare more equitable and efficient. The research also discusses challenges like data bias and the necessity for human oversight in sensitive scenarios, proposing strategies for effective implementation and continuous improvements.

Title: VietX-NLI: A Cross-lingual Natural Language Inference Dataset with Vietnamese as the Source Language
Abstract: Natural Language Inference (NLI) is a fundamental task in language understanding. While cross-lingual NLU has progressed rapidly, many multilingual datasets rely on English-centric translations, often failing to capture the linguistic and cultural nuances of target languages. Despite having over 100 million speakers, Vietnamese remains low-resource in NLP, especially in NLI. We introduce VietX-NLI, a new multilingual NLI dataset with Vietnamese as the source language. It contains over 100,000 premise-hypothesis pairs, translated into English and Chinese using Neural Machine Translation. Translation quality was validated using the Adequacy-Fluency Measure (AMFM), achieving an average score above 4.3/5. We benchmarked mBERT, XLM-R, mBART, and infoXLM, finding that XLMRlarge performed best (over 70% accuracy and F1-macro). VietXNLI provides a valuable resource for advancing NLI and cross-lingual understanding, particularly for Vietnamese speakers.

Title: Optimising SQL Generation for Afrikaans Through an English-to-Afrikaans Double Translation Method
Abstract: Neural Machine Translation (NMT) has achieved remarkable progress in translating languages with varying resource levels. However, the performance can be hindered by limited data availability and poor-quality corpora for low-resource languages (LRL). The aim of this study is to optimise SQL generation for Afrikaans through a “query double translation” method. Here, high-resource language (HRL) prompts (e.g., English) are translated to a LRL (e.g., Afrikaans) to improve SQL query generation. First, we evaluate three NMT models for English-to-Afrikaans translation, selecting the best-performing model to translate an English-to-SQL dataset. This dataset is then fine-tuned for Afrikaans-to-SQL conversion. The resulting model's performance is benchmarked against the original English SQL data and compared with two large language models (LLM). This study addresses NMT challenges in LRLs and highlights potential SQL generation improvements for underrepresented languages.

Title: Bridging Dialects: Enhancing Neural Machine Dialect Translation for Gujarati Language Through Model Adaptation
Abstract: Over the time, Natural Language Processing (NLP) has gained much prominence and also it has evolved in the way different approaches are used to design and implement the algorithms. One of the important tasks that can be performed with the help of NLP is of Machine Translation. While the Machine Translation systems are very much accurate in current scenario, there is still room for improvement in case of those languages which are low in resource. To solve the issue, this study is focused on development and assessment of a novel Neural Machine Translation (NMT) model which is specifically designed for the task of translating from Saurashtra Gujarati dialect to the Standard Gujarati dialect. While Gujarati is a low resource language, its dialectical variation of Saurashtra has even less available resources. So, to tackle this issue we undertake the creation of a self-generated supervised dataset with sentence pair of Saurashtra Gujarati sentence and standard Gujarati sentence, that helps in capturing the unique vocabulary and linguistic nuances of the Saurashtra Gujarati. For the NMT system, we are utilizing one of the recent developments by Meta which is NLLB (No Language Left Behind) model. It is used as the base architecture and then it is fine-tuned on the self-generated dataset that would help in capturing the complexities of Saurashtra Gujarati and enhancing the translation capabilities of the model. The results show that the NLLB model outperforms the MBART, GPT-4, and Gemini Advanced on evaluation metrics METEOR Score, BLEU Score, and ChrF Score by minimum 2% and maximum 14%. The results show that the NLLB is highly adaptive to low-resource language for dialect translation.

Title: Low-Resource English–Tigrinya MT: Leveraging Multilingual Models, Custom Tokenizers, and Clean Evaluation Benchmarks
Abstract: Despite advances in Neural Machine Translation (NMT), low-resource languages like Tigrinya remain underserved due to persistent challenges, including limited corpora, inadequate tokenization strategies, and the lack of standardized evaluation benchmarks. This paper investigates transfer learning techniques using multilingual pretrained models to enhance translation quality for morphologically rich, low-resource languages. We propose a refined approach that integrates language-specific tokenization, informed embedding initialization, and domain-adaptive fine-tuning. To enable rigorous assessment, we construct a high-quality, human-aligned English–Tigrinya evaluation dataset covering diverse domains. Experimental results demonstrate that transfer learning with a custom tokenizer substantially outperforms zero-shot baselines, with gains validated by BLEU, chrF, and qualitative human evaluation. Bonferroni correction is applied to ensure statistical significance across configurations. Error analysis reveals key limitations and informs targeted refinements. This study underscores the importance of linguistically aware modeling and reproducible benchmarks in bridging the performance gap for underrepresented languages. The resources are available https://github.com/hailaykidu/MachineT_TigEng

Title: Comparative Analysis of Neural Machine Translation Techniques for Sanskrit-to-English Using Deep Learning and Transformer Models
Abstract: This paper explores various experimental methods for training base models designed in deep learning and transformer methods for Sanskrit-to-English translation, focusing on improving translation quality and finding innovative training methods. Traditional approaches rely on limited datasets and predefined linguistic rules, which fail to capture the language’s full range of variations, resulting in suboptimal translation performance. To address this issue, we explore various training methods used for several types of datasets, including clean and raw data. Our experiments include training on clean as well as augmented raw datasets, and integrating attention mechanisms along with traditional architectures like GRU, LSTM and Transformer-based models. The best performing models were analyzed on the basis of accuracy metrics, among others, and found that GRU performed best when training for low resource language. The complex models seemed to perform much less as the requirement of adequate data is higher for them.

Title: Machine Translation Models for Low-resource Indo Aryan Languages: A Comprehensive Review of Techniques, Challenges and Future Scope
Abstract: Comparative studies of machine translation models for Indo-Aryan languages are given in this study. These languages are spoken by about 800 million people, but they still don't have enough computing power. Unlike larger studies that look at all Indian language groups, this one only looks at Indo-Aryan because it has a lot of the same typological problems and problems that affect other languages as well, like a lot of different scripts and morphologies and not enough parallel data. First, we put language features like SOV word order, complex inflectional systems, and the fact that scripts like Devanagari, Bengali, Odia, and Perso-Arabic exist together make translation pipelines more difficult. Then, we look at different paradigms, from early statistical machine translation systems that were based on rules and phrases to more modern neural approaches, such as RNN-based seq2seq, Transformer architectures, multilingual pre-trained models like IndicTrans, mBART, and mT5, and new large language models like GPT, BLOOM, and IndicLLM. The empirical base comes from datasets like IIT Bombay, Samanantar, and FLORES-200. Wikipedia and news text in one language are also used, but problems with domain mismatch and noise still exist. Automatic measures (BLEU, chrF, and COMET) are used in evaluation, along with human judgements of fluency, adequacy, and cultural alignment. The results show that multilingual Transformer-based models that use transfer from high-resource Hindi do a much better job of improving performance for low-resource languages like Odia and Assamese. Rule-based and SMT methods, on the other hand, are still not very good. Case studies show that there are benefits to transferring between scripts, but there are also problems that keep happening with grammar and idiomatic usage. Results show need for transfer, tuning, Bhashini for equal Indo-Aryan progress

Title: Automated Multilingual Content Delivery for the Visually Impaired via AI-Driven Document Parsing
Abstract: In multilingual societies, the challenge of accessing printed information remains acute for visually impaired individuals and non-native English speakers. This work introduces a sophisticated and extensible framework that unites advanced Optical Character Recognition (OCR) algorithms and neural machine translation, specifically engineered for English-to-Tamil conversion. In order to elevate recognition reliability, the methodology incorporates enhanced preprocessing techniques including adaptive thresholding and robust noise reduction algorithms, critically improving performance across diverse document types. Architecturally, the system integrates recent advances in character recognition, leveraging the open-source Tesseract engine and contemporary sequence-to-sequence translation models, with modularity for expansion to additional languages and features. Experimental validation utilizes a diverse array of datasets and is substantiated by standard metrics such as BLEU for translation fidelity. Comparative analyses with recent commercial and academic benchmarks are provided, and results are presented with comprehensive statistical analysis. The entire pipeline is implemented for accessible deployment, emphasizing usability, performance, and extensibility. The findings confirm highly competitive OCR accuracy and translation reliability, with particular suitability for resource-constrained environments and social inclusion efforts.

Title: TranslingoX: Real-Time Translation System for Indian Languages
Abstract: India's linguistic diversity creates communication challenges throughout the multilingual population. Title: Explicit Segmentation for Low-Resource NMT: A Case Study in QLoRA-Based Fine-Tuning of LLM for Khmer Language
Abstract: Neural Machine Translation (NMT) has significantly benefited high-resource languages, yet low-resource languages like Khmer continue to pose considerable challenges due to data scarcity and linguistic complexities, such as the lack of explicit word segmentation. This case study investigates the efficacy of the Gemma-3 family of models, specifically the Gemma3-1B-it and Gemma3-4B-it, for Khmer-English NMT. We compared zero-shot, few-shot, and QLoRA fine-tuning methods on both segmented and unsegmented text. Our findings show that fine-tuning is essential for this task. The fine-tuned Gemma3-4B-it model achieved a state-of-the-art BLEU score of 0.7418, significantly outperforming the zero-shot and few-shot approaches, which produced poor results. However, this peak performance comes with a latency trade-off: 21.24 s/iteration—about 7.1× slower than the faster but lower-quality zero-/few-shot baselines (≈2.69–3.30 s/iteration). This work provides a valuable benchmark and practical guidance on balancing translation quality and computational cost for under-resourced languages.

Abstract: This study advances real-time neural machine translation (NMT) by evaluating state-of-the-art Transformer models, including M2M100, NLLB-200, T5, and Marian-NMT across high and low resource languages (Spanish, Egyptian Arabic, and Chinese) using the FLORES-200 benchmark. We optimize cloud-based deployment through quantization and caching, achieving sub-2-second latency in our web application, InstaLingo. Our results demonstrate that architectural efficiency can outweigh model size. M2M100 outperforms Marian-NMT in Arabic translation for Egyptian (BLEU score: 10.37). Human evaluations also reveal a strong preference (85%) for context-sensitive translations over literal ones, underscoring the importance of semantic accuracy. Key challenges include computational constraints, the dialectal complexity of Egyptian Arabic, and the limitations of automated metrics (BLEU/ROUGE). This work highlights the feasibility of low-latency NMT while advocating for ethical, energy-efficient frameworks, and dialect-aware systems to address linguistic diversity. InstaLingo serves as a proof-of-concept, bridging theoretical research and practical implementation, with implications for human-centered evaluation and inclusive language support in real-time applications.

Title: Language Information Processing Algorithms in Intelligent Translation Systems
Abstract: Intelligent translation systems have key problems such as insufficient multi-language translation accuracy and high real-time requirements. Based on this, this paper combines cross-language word vectors to establish mapping relationships between low-resource languages, and introduces external professional dictionaries to enhance the translation consistency of domain terms. Transformer-based sequence modeling technology is adopted, and multi-head self-attention mechanism and position encoding are used to achieve global context perception. Bayesian optimization and grid search are combined to dynamically adjust hyperparameters, and mixed precision training is used to accelerate convergence. Beam search and length penalty are used to optimize the decoding process, and the reordering strategy is combined to improve the fluency of the target language. Compared with the traditional statistical machine translation (SMT) model, the average BLEU score of the translation system based on the Transformer model is about 93.15%, the TER score is lower, and the translation delay is reduced. This study effectively improves the accuracy and efficiency of translation and meets the needs of cross-language communication in different fields.

Title: Towards Human-Free Alignment for Low-Resource Machine Translation: Self-Supervised Preferences Meet Self-Reward Reinforcement Learning
Abstract: Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) has recently improved neural machine translation (MT), but it typically relies on costly human preferences or external quality estimation (QE) models and remains underexplored in genuinely low-resource settings. In this work, we propose a human-feedback-free alignment framework for low-resource MT that unifies self-supervised preferences with self-reward reinforcement learning on top of a 7B open-weight large language model. Starting from a small parallel corpus, Stage I performs supervised fine-tuning to obtain an MT-capable model that can both translate and self-correct. Stage II constructs preference pairs from monolingual source sentences via self-generated candidates and automatically derived wins/losses, and optimizes them with a DPO-style objective. Stage III further refines the model using a unified self-reward objective that jointly accounts for self-judged quality, preference consistency, and safety-aware penalties, without any human preference labels or external QE reward models. Experiments on En↔ Zh in low-resource configurations demonstrate that our aligned model achieves strong KIWI, XCOMET, and METRICX scores, consistently outperforming general-purpose open-weight LLMs and approaching or surpassing several MT-specialized systems. A controlled low-resource study shows that the gains are most pronounced when parallel data is scarce, yet remain robust as more supervision becomes available. Ablations on reward design analysis further reveal that self-supervised preferences and self-reward RL are complementary: the unified reward simultaneously improves adequacy and fluency, yielding a more faithful MT system under a human-feedback-free preference and reward alignment paradigm.

Title: Error Detection in English Machine Translation Using Fine Tuned NMT with Decision Trees Mechanism
Abstract: Language translation (CLT) is an automated systems that produce the translation from one natural language to another, without any human intervention. As the most of the resources are mostly available in English, multi-lingual translation is badly without any errors so that can deep dive into many applications. Neural machine translation (NMT) is one such intelligent technique which usually deployed for an efficient translation process from one source of language to another language. But these NMT techniques substantially requires the large corpus of data to achieve the improved translation process. Although specific languages have these NMT systems in place, creating one for low-resource languages is challenging due to the morphological attractiveness and nonavailability of the non-parallel corpus. To overcome this aforementioned problem, this research article proposes the modified transformer architecture for NMT to improve the translation efficiency of the NMT with the detecting the translation error accurately. The proposed NMT framework, consist of Encoder-Decoder architecture which consist of enhanced version of transformer architecture with the multiheaded decision trees attention networks. The proposed architecture learns words from the parallel corpus of data that it is trained on WMT-21 language vocabulary and its efficiency is measured by the evaluation metrics like Bilingual Evaluation Understudy (BLEU), character-level F-score (chrF) and Word Error Rate (WER). To prove the excellence of the proposed model, extensive comparison between the proposed and existing architectures is compared and its performance metrics are analysed. Results demonstrates that the proposed architecture has shown the improvised NMT by achieving the BLEU as 0.92 and low WER when compared to the exisiting models.

Title: Developing Phrase-Based SMT for low-Resource Language Translation: Myanmar and Tedim Chin Language
Abstract: This paper presents an initial evaluation of a translation system developed to address the linguistic gap between the Myanmar and Tedim Chin languages. As part of this project, we have also compiled a parallel corpus for Myanmar-Tedim Chin, containing around 50,000 sentences sourced from the UCSY corpus. Translation involves converting the symbols or characters of one writing system into those of another, with the aim of preserving the original pronunciation as closely as possible. For the Myanmar and Tedim Chin languages, accurate translation is particularly challenging due to the complexity of their writing systems and the limited availability of relevant data. In this study, we perform statistical experiments using the Phrase-Based Statistical Machine Translation (PBSMT) model, employing 5-gram language models during the decoding phase. We conduct experiments with a test set of 1,000 sentences and a development set of 7,000 sentences from the newly created dataset. To assess the performance of the translation system, we use the Bilingual Evaluation Understudy (BLEU) score, evaluating both Myanmar-to-Tedim Chin and Tedim Chin-to-Myanmar translation directions.

Title: Comparative Evaluation of RNN-based Bahdanau Attention vs Transformer Model for NMT in South African Low-Resource Languages
Abstract: The linguistic diversity of South Africa presents significant challenges for multilingual communication, particularly in resource-constrained environments such as customer call centers. This study uses South African low-resource language pairs to investigate and compare the performance of two prominent neural machine translation (NMT) architectures, namely the Bahdanau Attention Model and the Transformer Model with multi-headed self-attention. The study would illustrate which model performes best in translation between low-resource languages of South Africa. The study uses parallel corpora from JW300 and Autshumato datasets. Three language pairs were evaluated: isiZulu to Sesotho, Swati to Ndebele, and Tsonga to Setswana. The languages were selected to best cover the south African low resource languages families. The study adopts the Design Science Research Methodology (DSRM) for implementing two NMT architectures. Each model was trained under equivalent conditions and assessed using BLEU scores, sentence length distribution, and training time per epoch. Results indicate that the Transformer model consistently outperformed the attention-based model in translation accuracy (BLEU-4), while the attention model showed higher BLEU-1 scores in some instances, suggesting better word-level precision. The results also suggested that similarities in grammatical structure, vocabulary overlap, and sentence distribution patterns are pivotal in translation accuracy and contextual understanding.

Title: Vision Transformer-Based Image Captioning for the Visually Impaired
Abstract: Digital accessibility remains a central concern in Human-Computer Interaction (HCI), particularly for visually impaired individuals who depend on assistive technologies to interpret visual content. While image captioning systems have shown notable progress in high-resource languages, languages such as Indonesian, despite having a large speaker base, continue to be underserved. This disparity stems from the lack of annotated datasets and models that account for linguistic and cultural nuances, thereby limiting equitable access to visual information for Indonesian-speaking users. To address this gap, we present a bilingual image captioning framework aimed at improving digital accessibility for visually impaired users in the Indonesian-speaking community. We propose an end-to-end system that integrates a neural machine translation component with three deep learning-based captioning architectures: CNN-RNN, Vision Transformer with GPT-2 (ViT-GPT2), and Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs). The Flickr30k dataset was translated into Indonesian using leading machine translation models, with Google Translate achieving the highest scores across BLEU, METEOR, and ROUGE metrics. These translated captions served as training data for evaluating the image captioning models. Experimental results demonstrate that the ViT-GPT2 model outperforms the others, achieving the highest BLEU (0.2599) and ROUGE (0.3004) scores, reflecting its effectiveness in generating accurate and contextually rich captions. This work advances inclusive AI by developing culturally adaptive captioning models for underrepresented languages. By generating culturally and linguistically relevant captions for visually impaired users, the framework advances Human-Computer Interaction through more accessible and inclusive user-system communication. Beyond its technical contributions, this research addresses key challenges in Human-Computer Interaction (HCI) by enabling inclusive, multilingual assistive technologies. It supports the evolution of Next-Generation Work environments by equipping visually impaired individuals with tools to independently interpret visual information, an increasingly essential capability in AI-rich, visually oriented digital workspaces. In future work, the framework will be enhanced through multimodal pretraining and the integration of culturally enriched datasets, aiming to improve semantic accuracy and broaden its applicability to a wider range of linguistic communities.

Title: MT5-Based Multimodal Framework for Kannada-to-English Translation
Abstract: Our paper presents a multimodal kannada-to-english translation system based on the mT5large transformer model, fine-tuned on the AI4Bharat Samanantar dataset. Designed to support three input modalities—typed kannada text, images containing printed kannada script, and spoken kannada audio—the system facilitates seamless translation across diverse formats using a unified architecture. For image inputs, Tesseract OCR with the kannada language pack is used to extract text from scanned documents or photographs. For audio, the system employs OpenAI’s Whisper model to transcribe kannada speech into text with high fidelity. The extracted or directly entered text is then processed by the fine-tuned mT5 model to generate english translations. Our approach effectively integrates state-of-the-art technologies in Optical Character Recognition (OCR), Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR), and neural machine translation, demonstrating their combined utility in addressing the linguistic challenges associated with low-resource languages. Evaluation of the system yields a BLEU score of 0.5583, a ChrF score of 67.4113, and a TER score of 26, indicating competitive translation quality. The high accuracy across multiple input types highlights the robustness of the system and its ability to generalize across various forms of user interaction. Our research contributes toward inclusive language technologies by enabling kannada speakers to access digital content and services in english, thus supporting broader applications in education, accessibility, and public service delivery. The system exemplifies how multilingual and multimodal AI can bridge communication gaps in linguistically diverse societies like India.

Title: English-Hausa Question-Answer Parallel Corpus Development to Bridge the Low-Resource Gap
Abstract: Neural Machine Translation (NMT) for low-resource languages presents persistent challenges due to limited parallel corpora and significant morphological complexity of the language pairs. In this study, we describe the construction of English-Hausa Question Answering (QA) parallel corpus. A subset of 110,000 English QA pairs from VQA V2 dataset are translated manually to Hausa by native Hausa speakers who know English. Using these manual translations as ground truth, the performances of Google Translate and MarianMT in translating English to Hausa are evaluated based on automatic metrics (BLEU, chrF, TER) alongside human assessments of fluency, adequacy, naturalness, and cultural appropriateness. Results indicate that Google Translate slightly outperforms MarianMT with BLEU score (31.93 vs. 30.46), chrF score (47.23 vs. 45.75) and TER score (44.63 vs. 46.91), while MarianMT receives higher ratings in all human-evaluated dimensions, underscoring its contextual and cultural sensitivity. The manual Hausa translations are aligned with corresponding English corpus to create English-Hausa QA parallel corpus. This corpus is used to evaluate eight baselines. Among these baseline, Transformer + LSTM model delivers the strongest performance (BLEU: 74.90; chrF: 83.60; TER: 12.70), marginally outperforming a competitive RNN + GRU baseline without attention (BLEU: 74.00; chrF: 83.30; TER: 13.20). In contrast, Transformer-based models using Byte Pair Encoding (BPE) performed poorly (BLEU: 1.20-2.20), likely due to segmentation inconsistencies and optimization instability during training. The English-Hausa QA corpus provides a robust benchmark for future research in processing Hausa text.

Title: Analyzing Quantization in Multilingual Transformer Models for Indic Translation
Abstract: The growing adoption of multilingual sequence-to-sequence transformer models has significantly advanced neural machine translation (NMT), enabling support for hundreds of language pairs. However, their substantial computational and memory requirements hinder deployment in resource sparse environments. Post-Training Quantization (PTQ) addresses this by reducing model size and inference cost through low-precision representations. While PTQ has been studied for high-resource, Latin-script languages, its effects on translation tasks involving Indic languages remain underexplored. This work investigates how quantization impacts translation quality in morphologically rich, low-resource, non-Latin script languages, using Hindi as a representative case. This model evaluates three multilingual transformer models, mBART, M2M-100, and NLLB, under four quantization levels (FP32, FP16, INT8, and 4-bit) across three language pairs: English-French (high-resource Latin script), English-Galician (low-resource Latin script), and English-Hindi (low-resource Indic), using the FLORES-101 benchmark. Results show that Hindi often exhibits degradation levels comparable to or lower than Galician and even French. FP16 and INT8 quantization maintain strong translation quality, while 4-bit variants degrade significantly. Reverse translations (target language to English) consistently outperform forward translations. These findings suggest that moderate quantization is viable for Indic-language translation and that degradation is not solely dictated by language resource level or script. This work provides systematic observations of quantized multilingual translation for Indic languages, offering a foundation for future research in low-resource, non-Latin script NMT.

Title: Deep Learning-Based Image Processing for Tulu Script Identification
Abstract: Tulu is a South Dravidian language used in India's coastal Karnataka and northern Kerala, but it is far from being adequately represented in the digital sphere. This paper outlines an end-to-end deep learning-based Optical Character Recognition (OCR) and bidirectional translation of English and Tulu, with an aim to preserve and revive the language using AI tools. We propose a hybrid CNN-GRU model for handwritten Tulu character and digit recognition that is trained with a dataset of over 31,000 images manually hand-gathered for 62 classes. The system achieved an exceptional recognition accuracy of 94.12%, showing robustness even against varied handwriting styles. In order to improve model generalization, the dataset was augmented by rotation, zoom, and brightness modulation operations, while character localization was achieved through bounding box segmentation. The feature space was also investigated using PCA in order to offer class separability along with structural simplicity. To translate, we utilized a neural machine translation (NMT) pipeline based on an encoder-decoder architecture utilizing Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks. Trained on a parallel corpus of 1,000 English-Tulu sentence pairs, the model achieved a BLEU score of 0.83 for English-to-Tulu translation and 0.65 for Tulu-to-English, indicating robust contextual understanding under the low-resource environment. Together, these systems are the first end-to-end OCR and translation system for the Tulu language. In addition to technical contribution, this project contributes to larger goals of linguistic preservation and diversity AI, with a scalable platform for such efforts in other underrepresented languages.
