Title: Lost in Machine Translation: The Sociocultural Implications of Language Technologies in Nigeria
Abstract: In this paper, we explore machine translation within Nigerian contexts. We conducted 20 semi-structured interviews with native speakers of Ìgbò, Yorùbá, and Hausa that have used machine translation in professional settings. Our findings illustrate how machine translation applications face challenges within local Nigerian contexts and contribute to the loss of contextual meaning within Nigerian languages. Ultimately, English language dominance within MT tools decenters less commonly imagined uses for language technologies in Nigeria. We discuss how, if unmitigated, machine translation plays a distinctive role in the perpetuation of linguistic colonialism, epistemic violence, and the cultural erasure of low-resourced language communities.

Title: A Low-Power Neural Translation Accelerator: Hardware Architecture Design on Heterogeneous Computing Platforms
Abstract: With the widespread application of the neural machine translation (NMT) models in the field of multilingual semantic understanding, its dependence on computing resources and power consumption has become a major challenge for deployment on resource-constrained edge devices. Therefore, this study proposes a neural translation accelerator hardware architecture for low-power deployment. At the same time, combined with the optimization strategy of heterogeneous computing platforms, the comprehensive performance of NMT models in translation accuracy, energy efficiency, and inference latency is systematically improved. First, this study introduces a neural translation method based on k-nearest neighbor retrieval enhancement at the algorithm level. This algorithm enhances semantic consistency and improves the BLEU index through contextual prompt mechanism and dynamic confidence control. Secondly, in terms of hardware architecture, a heterogeneous node system integrating ARMv8 CPU and multi-core DSP is constructed. At the same time, a multi-level parallel training and inference mechanism is designed, and DVFS energy consumption modeling, task scheduling state vector and migration priority function are introduced. This operation can achieve energy-efficiency-aware load balancing and system scheduling. Through experimental verification on embedded heterogeneous platforms, the architecture has demonstrated excellent performance in multiple dimensions. In terms of BLEU translation accuracy, it has been improved by up to 9.1% compared with traditional models; in terms of energy efficiency, BLEU/W has been improved to 8.82 per unit power consumption; system latency and average task waiting time have been reduced by 15.7% and 26.3% respectively. Experimental results show that the proposed architecture design and its scheduling mechanism can effectively support the low-power and efficient deployment of NMT models in edge computing scenarios.

Title: Design and Development of Cross-Cultural English Communication Teaching Systems Based Hybrid Learning Algorithm
Abstract: Language is considered to be a powerful tool that connects the versatile cultures across the globe, thereby preserving their own customs and traditions. It is the best communication tool for imparting education even to the last man of society. Hence, an intelligent framework is required to extract the essence of the multiple languages and translate into English language, which would be essential to prepare the heritage-rich contents. In recent times, Neural Machine Translation (NMT) is used for translating the language texts from source language to target language, which enhances the user's ability to understand the other linguistic features. However, translating the low-resource remains to be complex bottleneck which prevents the existing education systems to penetrate the heritages of the other languages into their teaching academics. In this context, this research paper proposes the hybrid combination of Long Short-Term Memory and transformer-M2M model to translate the resource-constrained languages to English that aids for the better teaching process. The proposed framework is trained with Multi30k multimodal translation datasets. Consequently, performance of proposed model is calculated using Bilingual Evaluation Understudy (BLEU), character-level F-score (chF) and Word Error Rate (WER). To prove excellence of proposed model, extensive comparison between the proposed and existing architectures is compared and its performance metrics are analysed. Experimental results demonstrates that proposed architecture has achieved average of BLEU score of 0.94, chF of 0.9, and WER of 0.10 in converting the other languages to the English. The proposed network has shown the new paradigm in teaching systems for the students to explore the cultures and traditions of the other languages that improves the mental ability of the students.

Title: Advances in Machine Translation: A Comprehensive Survey of Large Language Models
Abstract: The conventional line of machine translation (MT) has been revolutionized by the advent of large language models (LLMs) that have dramatically increased translation performance on multi languages. In this survey, we conduct a thorough analysis of how and why LLMs have both developed and been applied to the problem of machine translation. The paper investigates these basic models including Transformer, mBART, and GPT, as well as recent advances such as zero shot and few shot learning capabilities. Multilingual translation, domain adaptation and dealing with low resource languages are all given special treatment. We discuss key challenges, like scalability, model interpretability, and bias mitigation, and potential solutions. The survey also sheds light on how MT is merging with emotion detection, in real time translation and surprisingly, integrating multimodal inputs from humans. In general, this work seeks to provide a view into the current landscape concerning opportunities and potential future directions with which LLMs can augment existing machine translation systems.

Title: Parameter Efficient Fine-Tunning of LLMs: Application to Machine Translation from English to Portuguese
Abstract: Fine-tuning Large Language Models (LLMs) for specific tasks, such as machine translation, is a computationally expensive process that often requires substantial hardware resources. Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) methods, such as Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) and Quantized Low-Rank Adaptation (QLoRA), offer a resource-efficient alternative by significantly reducing the number of trainable parameters and memory requirements. In this work, we compare the performance and memory efficiency of LoRA and QLoRA on English-Portuguese translation tasks, utilizing two cutting edge LLMs, Meta LLaMA 3.1 8B and Mistral 7B. Our experiments demonstrate that both LoRA and QLoRA achieve substantial memory savings. Moreover, this work underscores the practical advantages of LoRA and QLoRA in resource-constrained environments, providing a foundation for further optimization and experimentation in machine translation using large language models.

This study sets a new benchmark in machine translation, paving the way for future research on multilingual data and fine-tuning techniques.

Title: A Novel Rule-Based Knowledge Representation Model for Machine Translation
Abstract: Machine translation is one of the major areas in computational linguistics that involves the use of computer algorithms to automatically translate text between natural languages. The emergence of Large Language Models (LLMs) has revolutionized the field of machine translation by marking a major turning point in its evolution. Despite the impressive capabilities of LLMs, they are unable to achieve human-like translation due to key limitations such as lack of transparency, explainability, and interpretability, non- deterministic outputs, and inadequate support for low-resource languages. Therefore, a promising solution can be proposed by incorporating humanaided translation mechanisms that reflect how the human brain performs translation. From a computer science standpoint, a promising solution is the development of a novel hybrid machine translation approach that integrates rule-based techniques with LLM-based methods. This paper introduces a novel rule-based knowledge representation model that is designed to accurately analyze source language input and structure the resulting linguistic information in a systematic format and facilitating applications such as target language generation and question answering systems. The system is comprised of four key modules namely preprocessor, morphological analyzer, syntax analyzer and semantic analyzer. Furthermore, the system has been successfully designed and implemented as a web-based application using Python language whereas all the NLP tasks related to this system have been modeled by using spaCy. Finally, the functionality of the system has been demonstrated through the development of a prototype question-answering system.

Title: Fine-Tuning Pretrained Language Models for Extremely Low-Resource Machine Translation: The Case of Makassarese-Indonesian
Abstract: Machine translation plays a vital role in enhancing accessibility and supporting the preservation of endangered languages by enabling cross-linguistic communication and expanding their presence in digital spaces. One such language is Makassarese, a regional language of Indonesia spoken by over three million people, yet it lacks sufficient representation in most major NLP datasets and is currently classified as threatened. To address this gap, this study investigates the effectiveness of fine-tuning pretrained language models (PLMs) for machine translation involving the extremely low-resource Makassarese language. Two PLMs—mBART-large-50 and IndoBART-v2—were evaluated on the bidirectional translation task between Makassarese and Indonesian. Experiments were conducted using three dataset configurations with distinct characteristics. Results indicate that the multilingual mBART-large-50 model performs better when dealing with diverse linguistic styles, predominantly informal contexts, and longer sentences. Meanwhile, the monolingual IndoBART-v2 model shows superior performance on datasets with shorter sentences and formal language styles. These findings highlight the potential of fine-tuning PLMs to improve translation quality in extremely low-resource and unseen language scenarios.

Title: Exploration of Vocabulary Expansion and Self-Supervised Enhancement Methods for Han-Zhuang Machine Translation
Abstract: This paper proposes a low-resource translation method that integrates vocabulary expansion and multi-noise self-supervised enhancement, to address the bottlenecks of insufficient parallel corpora, limited vocabulary coverage, and weak model generalization in Han(Chinese)-Zhuang machine translation. First, the Zhuang vocabulary is expanded based on the BPE vocabulary of sub-word units to alleviate out-of-vocabulary issues in low-resource scenarios. Second, noisy self-supervised pre-training is performed on the Zhuang monolingual corpus, designing various perturbation strategies such as masking, deletion, insertion, shuffling, and reversal to significantly improve the model’s language modeling capabilities and robustness. Finally, the language model is fine-tuned based on the limited Han-Zhuang parallel corpus. Experimental results demonstrate that this method achieves significant improvements in translation quality assessment metrics, such as the standardized BLEU metric SacreBLEU, character F-score (ChrF), and translation error rate (TER). SacreBLEU increases by approximately 4.70 to 53.09, ChrF increases by 2.51 to 73.28, and TER decreases by approximately 6.99 to 36.76. Research shows that this method framework provides a scalable technical path for machine translation of low-resource or even extremely low-resource languages, expanding the boundaries of cross-language intelligent processing.

Title: Effectiveness of Transfer Learning Approach for Low-Resource Bangla Dialect Translation
Abstract: The Chittagonian dialect is largely used in the Chittagong region of Bangladesh. The lack of data makes translating Chittagonian dialects extremely challenging. Even so, the problem of data scarcity is lessened when transfer learning is incorporated into pretrained models. The linguistic richness of both standard Bangla and the Chittagonian dialect makes machine translation more difficult. Without a large amount of data, machine translation models often perform badly. The purpose of this study is to compare the performance results of the suggested models and apply transfer learning for efficient machine translation. With an emphasis on the effects of fine-tuning in a dataset with minimal data, this research investigates the efficiency of encoder-decoder-based models in translating the low-resource Chittagonian dialect. For dialect translation in this research, we used fine-tuned mBART, NLLB, and mT5 models along with transfer learning, and even though we kept the tuning parameter constant, we witnessed distinct variations in the models’ performances. This was evident when the Bilingual Evaluation Understudy (BLEU) score, Word Error Rate (WER), and Character Error Rate (CER) differed significantly. The accuracy of the NLLB model was the highest of the three models, with a BLEU score of 82.67, 8.25% WER, and 4.77% CER.

Title: Intelligent Assistance in English Teaching: An Adaptive Error Correction System Based on Machine Translation Assessment
Abstract: In view of the fact that existing machine translation error correction tools used in English teaching do not pay enough attention to differences in translation quality, leading to problems such as over-correction or under-correction, this paper proposes an adaptive error correction system based on machine translation evaluation for intelligent auxiliary English teaching. The system builds a “quality perception-dynamic error correction” closed-loop mechanism, integrating a machine translation quality evaluation module, an error correction module, and an adaptive adjustment module. The quality evaluation module identifies error probabilities at the word level and overall quality scores at the sentence level in students' English translations. The error correction module, drawing on advanced language processing technologies, adjusts its focus according to quality information to target errors more precisely. The adaptive adjustment module optimizes its performance based on feedback from correction results. Experiments were conducted on English learning datasets, including students' compositions, translation exercises, and daily communication dialogues. The results show that the proposed system performs significantly better in correcting English errors than traditional tools: on standard English-Chinese translation practice materials, its correction accuracy is 2.8 % higher than common QE-guided correction tools, and the rate of unnecessary changes is $\text{2. 2 \%}$ lower, in low-resource scenarios such as colloquial English dialogues, its accuracy is $\text{2. 7 \%}$ higher than comparative tools. Control experiments show that removing the adaptive adjustment module leads to $\mathrm{2}. \mathrm{3} \%$ drop in correction accuracy. The system can accurately handle various English errors such as grammar, semantics, and terminology use. While ensuring correction accuracy, it processes long sentences 8.3 % faster than common large-scale correction tools, balancing accuracy and efficiency, making it suitable for multiple English teaching scenarios such as writing, translation, and oral practice.

Title: Towards Resilient Multimodal Machine Translation for English–Hindi Employing the Mistral-B Architecture
Abstract: Multimodal machine translation (MMT) combines the textual and visual data to enhance translation quality, particularly for low-resource languages like Hindi. This paper presents an MMT system for English-to-Hindi translation using the Multi30k dataset and the Mistral-B model, a transformer-based architecture optimized for multimodal tasks. We evaluate the system’s performance using the BLEU score, a standard metric for assessing translation quality. Our experiments demonstrate that the Mistral-B model, when fine-tuned on the Multi30k dataset, achieves competitive BLEU scores, highlighting the efficacy of multimodal approaches in improving translation accuracy for English-to-Hindi language pairs. The results underscore the potential of integrating visual context to address linguistic ambiguities in low-resource settings.The reliance on the Multi30k dataset limits the generalizability of the results, as it is small, caption-focused, and not truly representative of real-world English–Hindi translation tasks. Furthermore, the evaluation is restricted to BLEU scores without incorporating semantic or human-centered metrics, raising concerns about the comprehensive assessment of translation quality. These limitations highlight key research gaps for the NLP community, such as the need for larger multimodal Hindi corpora, advanced evaluation metrics beyond BLEU, and improved fusion architectures for effectively integrating visual and textual features. These challenges also open avenues for benchmarking initiatives and low-resource adaptability studies, thereby guiding future research in multimodal machine translation.

Title: A Rule-Based Machine Translation Framework for Low-Resource Language Pairs
Abstract: Translation is not just about linguistic accuracy; it requires cultural sensitivity to preserve idiomatic expressions, cultural references, and syntactic structures unique to each language. Translating from Hindi, one of India's most widely spoken languages, to Tulu, a Dravidian language with a rich cultural and oral tradition, presents specific challenges. Tulu's colloquial phrases, cultural nuances, and emotional depth often get lost in translation, as existing tools like Google Translator, Galaxy.ai, and Lang-Lation fail to provide contextually accurate or grammatically precise translations. These tools highlight the limitations of current techniques, which often lack the ability to handle low-resource language pairs effectively. This paper identifies key challenges such as handling orthographic variations, capturing contextual meaning, and adapting cultural nuances while maintaining grammatical accuracy. To address these challenges, we propose a Rule-Based Machine Translation (RBMT) system tailored specifically for Hindi-to-Tulu translation. The system focuses on linguistic fidelity, cultural adaptation, and robust handling of syntactic and morphological differences. By leveraging curated linguistic rules, a bilingual dictionary, and advanced preprocessing techniques, this research aims to bridge the linguistic gap between Hindi and Tulu while preserving their cultural essence. The findings not only demonstrate the system's ability to produce more accurate translations but also emphasize the need for customized approaches to support low-resource language pairs in machine translation.

Title: Construction of a Recurrent Neural Network Machine Translation Framework Based on Data Enhancement and Attention Mechanisms
Abstract: In order to improve the semantic modeling ability and translation quality of recurrent neural networks in machine translation tasks, a neural translation framework that incorporates data enhancement and multi-level attention mechanisms is constructed. The research design includes text-level semantic perturbation, language model-based context generation strategy and gated recalibration with multi-scale context fusion in the attention enhancement module, which systematically improves the model’s generalization performance and semantic alignment accuracy in low-resource environments. Comparison experiments on the WMT14 English-German dataset show that the constructed model outperforms the baseline model in BLEU, perplexity and syntactic coverage, especially in long sentence translation and complex syntactic structure processing, which verifies the effectiveness of the structural optimization and strategy integration.

Title: A Multi-Time and Multi-Perspective Selection Framework for Machine Translation based on Large Language Models
Abstract: The rapid development of large language models (LLMs) has brought unprecedented capabilities to machine translation systems, yet their probabilistic generation nature introduces significant variability in output quality. This inherent randomness poses substantial challenges for real-world applications where consistent and reliable translations are crucial. To mitigate this issue, we present a novel Multi-time and Multi-perspective Selection Framework (MMSF) that systematically enhances translation stability through an innovative combination of parallel generation and comprehensive evaluation. Our approach begins by generating multiple candidate translations through a unified prompt design, avoiding limitations of single-generation methods. For example, prompts may explicitly request multiple variants or leverage temperature sampling to encourage diversity. Each candidate then undergoes rigorous multi-dimensional assessment, evaluating critical aspects such as semantic fidelity, linguistic fluency, stylistic coherence, and domain-specific terminology accuracy. The framework employs advanced normalization techniques to ensure fair comparison across these diverse evaluation dimensions, while a unique bidirectional verification mechanism further validates translation quality through semantic consistency checks. Importantly, this methodology achieves substantial quality improvements without requiring computationally expensive model retraining or fine-tuning. The effectiveness of MMSF has been thoroughly validated across a wide range of language pairs and translation scenarios, with particularly notable performance gains observed in complex linguistic contexts and low-resource settings. By providing a systematic approach to harnessing the full potential of LLMs for translation tasks, this work offers practitioners a practical and efficient solution for achieving more stable and reliable machine translation outputs in production environments.

Title: Exploring Transfer Learning in a Bidirectional Myanmar-Tedim Chin Machine Translation with the mT5 Transformer
Abstract: Machine translation (MT) plays a crucial role in bridging linguistic gaps, particularly for underrepresented languages. This paper investigates the feasibility and performance of the mT5-transformer model in machine translation task from Myanmar to Tedim Chin and Tedim Chin to Myanmar language respectively. Title: LLM-based Formality Ranking of Candidate Translations
Abstract: It is important for a translated text to have an appropriate level of formality for the target reader. To meet this need, formality-controlled machine translation systems have been trained to generate both formal and informal outputs. However, this binary choice may not be sufficient for the nuanced levels of formality required in many real-world contexts. A wider choice of candidate translations, potentially taken from various sources and systems, would be useful for translators and post-editors. To facilitate their review, it would be helpful to indicate the relative level of formality of these translations. This paper investigates the use of Large Language Models for automatic ranking of candidate translations according to formality, especially for low-resource languages that do not have large-scale training data. We performed experiments on a Mandarin-Cantonese parallel corpus in which the Cantonese translations are ranked by formality. Results show that the chain-of-thought prompting method attains the best correlation with human rankings, and that it is robust in identifying the most formal and most informal sentences in the face of machine translation errors.

Title: Machine Translation of Comics with Visual Reconstruction for Linguistic Accessibility
Abstract: This paper presents a computational approach for the machine translation of comic book texts, aiming to promote linguistic accessibility, particularly in emerging countries. Title: Chain-of-Morphemes Tuning: Injecting Morphology in LLM-based Machine Translation
Abstract: Generative Large Language Models (LLMs) have recently achieved remarkable advancements in translation tasks. However, low-resource or unseen language words are underrepresented in the LLM vocabulary where words are frequently constructed from subwords that may not align with their morphological structures. In this study, we present a novel two-stage morphological knowledge injection strategy into LLMs to address the difficulties presented by low-resource, agglutinative languages focusing on English-Manipuri translation as a case study. The first stage involves extending the LLM vocabulary with morphemes and segmenting Manipuri words into fine-grained morphological units that preserve morpheme boundaries in the input representation. The second stage introduces a chain-of-morphemes (CoM) tuning approach that divides the translation process into two steps: first, generating word roots for semantic translation, and then applying morphological inflection. This methodology decouples semantic and morphological processing, improving translation quality. Evaluation on the WMT 2023 English-Manipuri dataset using mGPT and BLOOM models demonstrates that our approach outperforms existing baseline methods. Our findings emphasize the potential advantages of incorporating morphological knowledge in LLM-based machine translation for morphologically rich languages.

Title: CLCO: Enhancing Chinese-Centric Low-Resource Machine Translation Through Domain-Specific Corpus Optimization
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) face significant challenges in machine translation (MT) between Chinese and low-resource languages (LRLs) within specialized domains, with the core constraint being the severe scarcity and imbalanced distribution of high-quality, domain-specific bilingual parallel corpora. To fundamentally optimize training data, we propose CLCO (Chinese-centric Low-resource Corpus Optimization), a two-stage, data-centric framework designed to build and refine domain-specific corpora at scale. In the first stage, a domain classifier is employed to filter large-scale general corpora, preliminarily extracting domain-relevant bilingual data. In the second stage, to address the issue of poor quality in the initially filtered data, a LLM is introduced to perform bidirectional back-translation (BT), generating diverse candidate sentence pairs. The optimal samples are then selected based on automated semantic similarity scoring, thereby refining the corpus quality. Extensive experiments on four Chinese-LRL pairs across two specialized domains demonstrate that fine-tuned LLMs on CLCO-optimized corpora achieve superior overall performance, with BLEU and COMET scores significantly outperforming established baselines, including zero-shot translation, direct fine-tuning, and direct optimization. These results strongly affirm that systematic corpus optimization is indispensable for achieving robust and domainadaptive low-resource translation.

Title: Sentiment Insights and Usability Evaluation for KADUMALIN Translation System
Abstract: Machine Translation (MT) has evolved and become necessary with the rise of generative AI. However, the effort to preserve a low-resource language such as Kadazandusun in Sabah becomes a challenge due to the informal Malay Sabahan slang, improper spellings, and sentiment used by younger generations, hence affecting the translation’s accuracy. This paper presents a user-centered evaluation of Kadumalin, an NLP-based machine translation system with spell checker features. We conducted a post-use survey analysis using the System Usability Scale (SUS) with 250 participants where Kadumalin achieved an average SUS score of 66.2, which indicates towards acceptable benchmark level of usability standard. Next, user feedback responses were analyzed to understand sentiment insights by comparing the lexical, machine learning, and hybrid deep learning sentiment analysis models. Our proposed hybrid BERT+XGBoost model with improved weight optimization achieved an FI (macro) score of 0.941608, encouraging results even on a small, imbalanced dataset. Positive feedback supported our effort to preserve the Kadazandusun language and its easy access. Negative feedback pointed out occasional mistranslations caused by limited corpus data, while neutral comments suggested improvements to the user interface design. These findings provide actionable insights for improving MT usability by combining SUS with sentiment analysis task in evaluating NLP-based solutions.

Title: Advancing Hausa Machine Translation: Linguistic Insights, Technological Innovations, and Pathways to Chinese Integration
Abstract: Machine Translation (MT) has significantly advanced from rule-based methods to sophisticated neural architectures. Low-resource languages like Hausa face considerable challenges due to linguistic complexities, limited datasets, and technological constraints. This paper reviews the linguistic intricacies of Hausa, including its agglutinative morphology, tonal system, and extensive dialectal variations, and examines their impact on MT systems. It highlights the similarities and challenges of integrating Hausa with Chinese in MT, considering the unique features of both languages, such as tonal systems and syntactic structures. Current MT development strategies, including neural, statistical, and hybrid approaches, are discussed in the context of low-resource languages. Proposed solutions focus on tone-aware mechanisms and context-sensitive models. Strategies for addressing data scarcity, such as back-translation and neural data augmentation, are assessed. The paper reviews evaluation methodologies, emphasizing both quantitative metrics like Bilingual Evaluation Understudy (BLEU), Translation Edit Rate (TER), Metric for Evaluation of Translation with Explicit Ordering (METEOR) and human-centric approaches, and discusses their specific relevance to Hausa and Chinese MT. By synthesizing these insights, this review provides actionable strategies to enhance translation quality and accessibility for Hausa, Chinese, and other low-resource languages. The paper concludes by emphasizing the potential of inclusive MT systems to mitigate linguistic, cultural, and socioeconomic disparities, improve equitable access to information, and facilitate global communication.

Title: Chinese-Tibetan Machine Translation with LoRA Fine-Tuning in Large Language Models
Abstract: Chinese-Tibetan machine translation plays a critical role in preserving Tibetan cultural heritage and promoting cross-lingual bilingual communication, yet it faces three key challenges in practical application: the scarcity of high-quality parallel corpora that limit model training, high computational costs of full-model fine-tuning, and insufficient cross-lingual adaptation capabilities caused by structural differences between Chinese and Tibetan. To resolve these constraints, this study applies the Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) lightweight tuning technique on the LlamaFactory platform, selecting two lightweight large language models (LLMs)—Qwen3-1.7B-base and DeepSeek-R1-DistillQwen-1.5B—as base models, and conducting supervised fine-tuning separately for the Tibetan→Chinese and Chinese→Tibetan translation directions; performance evaluation adopts four mainstream machine translation metrics (BLEU, ROUGE-1, ROUGE-2, ChrF) to comprehensively measure translation accuracy and fluency. Experimental results show that LoRA fine-tuning significantly improves the performance of both models: the DeepSeek model’s BLEU score increases from 1.55 to 18.11 in the Tibetan→Chinese direction and from 4.17 to 29.14 in the Chinese→Tibetan direction, while the Qwen model’s BLEU score rises from 0.97 to 3.17 in the Tibetan→Chinese direction and from 2.83 to 14.78 in the Chinese→Tibetan direction; notably, LoRA only tunes 0.0019% of the base model’s parameters (approximately 32k parameters), achieving performance comparable to full-model fine-tuning while reducing computational costs by over 99%, which effectively addresses the cost issue in low-resource language translation model tuning. This study makes three key contributions: it proposes a LoRA-based fine-tuning framework adapted to low-resource Chinese-Tibetan translation scenarios and verifies its effectiveness through experiments, conducts the first comparative study on the translation performance of two lightweight LLMs in bidirectional Chinese-Tibetan translation to provide a reference for subsequent model selection in related fields, and constructs a small-scale yet high-quality bilingual corpus covering news and daily dialogue fields—this corpus enriches data support for low-resource minority language translation research, while the work as a whole demonstrates the application potential of lightweight tuning techniques in this domain and provides a replicable research paradigm for studies on other minority language pairs such as Mongolian-Chinese and Uyghur-Chinese.

Title: LoRA-Fine Tuned LLaMA-3 for Low-Resource Multilingual Machine Translation
Abstract: This paper describes a multilingual machine translation system that uses Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) to finetune Meta’s LLaMA-3 (8B parameters) to translate low- and medium-resource languages. The study focuses on English (EN) to French (FR), Hindi (HI), Luganda (LG), and Spanish (ES) using limited parallel data to support high-quality translation. The system was trained on a low (3 million) number of sentence pairs from JW300 and OSCAR corpora. Training employs an extensive preprocessing pipeline (cleaning, normalisation, and subword tokenisation with LLaMA-3’s large (128k) SentencePiece vocabulary) and utilises LoRA adapters with QLoRA (4bit quantisation) for efficient finetuning. The finetuned model achieves competitive results on the FLORES-200 dev set for EN to FR, EN to HI, and EN to LG, despite finetuning .01 percent of the model parameters, with BLEU scores of 35.2, 18.4, and 12.1, respectively. Additional evaluations are provided using ChrF, TER, and BERTScore metric evaluations, and the results are discussed in consideration of resource availability. It is reported that the training loss curve typically stabilises after 50k training steps, indicating convergence, and the loss trade-offs for quantisation are examined. In addition, several techniques are experimented with to improve translation quality, including data augmentation with back-translation and filtering the corpus before training the model, which resulted in statistically significant gains, especially for the lowest-resource pair (EN - LG). The paper also discusses reflections on lessons learned for parameter-efficient adaptation in multilingual translation and future work towards universal translation models.

Abstract: Natural Language Processing (NLP) models have achieved remarkable accuracy in multiple areas such as named entity recognition, machine translation, and sentiment analysis. The impact of adversarial attacks has been studied mostly on high-resource languages. Low-resource languages, specifically Indian regional languages, are largely unexplored for these. This study exposes the NLP models trained on Indian regional languages to adversarial attacks, reveals the neural net vulnerabilities and seeks to defend, strengthen and mitigate these vulnerabilities.

Title: Natural Language Processing for Uzbek and Turkmen: A Systematic Review of Resources, Methods, and Benchmarks
Abstract: This review surveys the current state of Natural Language Processing for Uzbek and Turkmen, two closely related Turkic languages with agglutinative morphology, rich derivation, and recent script transitions. We synthesize publicly available resources (monolingual, parallel, and speech corpora), preprocessing practices (script normalization, language identification, and de-duplication), and modeling strategies ranging from finite-state morphology and classical sequence labeling to modern multilingual transformer baselines with task-specific fine-tuning. The task coverage includes morphological analysis, part-of-speech tagging, named-entity recognition, machine translation, and speech technologies such as automatic speech recognition and text-to- speech. We highlight an asymmetry in resource maturity—Uzbek has growing datasets and models, whereas Turkmen remains markedly under-resourced—and examine where cross-lingual transfer, joint subword vocabularies, and bilingual adapter techniques can bridge this gap. The paper contributes (i) a paired, comparative synthesis for Uzbek and Turkmen; (ii) a practical, reproducible baseline recipe that specifies data curation, subword tokenization with the SentencePiece library, multilingual transformer adapters, and evaluation using standard machine-translation and token-level precision-recall based scores; and (iii) a roadmap for community benchmarks with transparent training, development, and test splits and broad multilingual coverage. We also catalog gaps in Turkmen orthographic resources and propose cost-effective data acquisition strategies, including targeted web scraping, community sourcing, and dictionary- guided alignment. Ethical considerations around dialectal variation, domain bias, and privacy in web-scale data are discussed. Our findings indicate that modest, data-centric interventions—normalization across scripts, active learning, and high-quality filtering—often yield larger gains than architectural complexity, and that carefully designed shared tasks can catalyze comparable progress across both languages.

Title: Context-based Word Definition Classification for Arabic: Leveraging Pre-trained Language Models
Abstract: This research addresses the challenge of context-based word definition classification, a critical task in Natural Language Processing (NLP), particularly for morphologically rich languages like Arabic. Using a dataset of 3,670 annotated examples, we propose a methodology combining pre-trained BERT embeddings with cosine similarity to evaluate the contextual alignment of ambiguous word senses. Our approach achieved 80% accuracy, outperforming traditional methods like Word2Vec and Lesk by a significant margin. These findings highlight the potential of pre-trained transformers for tasks such as machine translation, information retrieval, and conversational AI in low-resource languages. Limitations include computational demands and limited gloss coverage, which will be addressed in future work by expanding resources and refining classification techniques for dialectal and multi-lingual scenarios.

Title: A Comprehensive Survey on Machine Transliteration Techniques and Trends
Abstract: Machine transliteration is an essential task within multilingual Natural Language Processing (NLP), facilitating the phonetic transformation of text across various scripts. It is crucial for applications such as cross-lingual information retrieval, machine translation, and named entity recognition, especially for languages that are resource-constrained. This survey synthesizes developments in transliteration techniques from early rule-based and statistical approaches to current neural and transformer-based models. We categorize major methodologies, review widely used datasets and evaluation metrics, and highlight the strengths and limitations of rule-driven, probabilistic, neural, and hybrid paradigms. Furthermore, the paper highlights emerging trends and delineates future pathways aimed at enhancing transliteration performance. Finally, we concluded consolidate understanding of existing and emerging directions in machine transliteration area, which offers guidance for both practical stakeholders and academics.

Title: LAFAEK-Corpus-1M+: A Large-Scale Tetun Corpus to Build a Low-Resourced LLM for Speech and Text Processing
Abstract: This paper introduces a Tetun text corpus Lafaek-Corpus-1M+. A Large Language Model (LLM) has attracted full attention in natural language processing and speech processing. To build an LLM, huge corpora are basically needed, however, it is quite hard for low-resourced languages. We focus on one Asian language Tetun, and make a text corpus for a Tetun LLM. We collect more than million Tetun sentences from various resources. After that, we applied continual pre-training to a Llama-3.1 model using our corpus to build a Tetun LLM. We conducted machine translation experiments. It is found that our LLM achieved better performance than the original model, and the effectiveness of our corpus is clarified.

Title: Empowering Access to Public Services: An Analysis on Multimodal, Retrieval-Augmented Chatbots for Indic Language Support to Farmers
Abstract: Rural communities in India face persistent barri-ers-linguistic diversity, low digital and language literacy, and limited domain-specific resources-when accessing government welfare information. This survey reviews advances in generative AI, retrieval-augmented generation, and multimodal chatbot systems for low-resource Indic languages, centered on the development of a remote-accessible assistant supporting voice, text, and image queries. We examine methods for unifying multimodal inputs, improving machine translation and information retrieval in chat-based frameworks, and grounding responses in official policy content. Key challenges include dialectal variation, data scarcity, and cost-efficient deployment at scale. By synthesizing current research and identifying gaps, this work provides design directions for robust, inclusive AI chatbots that bridge information accessibility gaps in rural India.

Title: Development and Evaluation of a Small Kazakh Language Corpus to Improve the Efficiency of Multilingual NLP Systems in Low-Resource Environments
Abstract: This study tackles NLP challenges in low-resource settings by developing the Small Kazakh Language Corpus—a high-quality, annotated collection of Kazakh texts sourced from news, scientific publications, and Wikipedia. The corpus was used to fine-tune two models for masked language modeling: the multilingual XLM-RoBERTa-base and the Kazakh-specific nur-dev/roberta-kaz-large. Fine-tuning notably improved XLM-RoBERTa-base's accuracy from 48.84% to 68.85% and F1-score from 41.96% to 68.62%, while nur-dev/roberta-kaz-large showed more modest gains. These findings demonstrate the critical role of language-specific resources in enhancing multilingual NLP systems and provide a solid foundation for further research in applications such as machine translation, sentiment analysis, and question answering.

Title: Embedded Language Translation Based on GRU Gated Attention Model
Abstract: The project "Embedded Language Translation Based on GRU Gated Attention Model" aims to develop an advanced machine translation system that seamlessly integrates Gated Recurrent Units (GRUs) with sophisticated attention mechanisms. This innovative model is specifically designed to handle sequential data effectively, addressing the common challenges of translating long sequences and maintaining contextual accuracy. By leveraging the selective focus capabilities of the attention mechanism, our system ensures more precise and contextually relevant translations. The comprehensive methodology includes meticulous data collection and preprocessing, model design and training, rigorous evaluation and fine-tuning, and seamless integration into resource-constrained environments such as mobile devices and IoT platforms. The ultimate goal is to deliver a robust, scalable, and high-performance embedded translation solution that can operate in real-time, thereby breaking language barriers and enhancing global communication.

Title: Dependent syntactic analysis of Mongolian based on semi-supervised self-training
Abstract: The analysis of Mongolian dependency syntax has always been an important part of Mongolian semantic analysis, machine translation, semantic role annotation and other tasks. However, the corpus of Mongolian as a low-resource language dependency syntax is very scarce. This paper proposes a new method for analysing Mongolian dependency syntax. The seq2seq model structure is employed for dependency syntax analysis of Mongolian, taking advantage of its morphological features and grammatical structure. However, the scarcity of a Mongolian corpus and the numerous parameters of other deep learning networks can result in overfitting. To address this challenge, a two-stage self-training framework is employed in conjunction with a confidence dynamic threshold setting method to construct a corpus of Mongolian dependent syntax. The experimental results demonstrate that the scores of dependent syntactic analysis in Labeled Attachment Score (LAS) and the Unlabeled Attachment Score (UAS) reach 86.65% and 85.80%, respectively.

Title: Automatic Identification and Translation of the French Impersonal Pronoun on into Jordanian Arabic
Abstract: The French impersonal pronoun on presents persistent challenges for machine translation (MT) and pronoun resolution due to its highly context-dependent referential scope and lack of a direct equivalent in many languages. Building on a previous qualitative study, we develop a translational NLP pipeline to detect, classify, and translate instances of on into Jordanian Arabic (JoA). Using a bilingual corpus of 200 French sentences and 400 JoA translations, we fine-tune three transformer models (mBART50, NLLB-200, LLaMA-3) and incorporate linguistic constraints through rule-based prompting and post-editing. Strategy-level accuracy increases from 61.8% to 84.7%, and BLEU scores improve from 23.4 to 27.1. Classroom deployment in a graduate course halves instructor correction time and boosts student translation accuracy by 19%. The study highlights the synergy between functional linguistics and explainable GenAI for low-resource dialectal MT.

Title: Interactive Pretraining-Based Framework for Hindi-Chinese Parallel Sentence Pairs Extraction
Abstract: Information retrieval and machine translation performance is often unsatisfactory in low-resource languages, primarily due to the limited availability of bilingual parallel corpora for training models. Hindi, as a typical low-resource language, faces an acute scarcity of bilingual parallel data, especially in relation to Chinese, which hinders the representation capabilities of parallel sentence extraction models. To tackle this issue, this paper presents a framework that combines interactive and pretrained language models to extract parallel sentences. The framework incorporates architectural structure and training data generation, and is evaluated from closed and open perspectives using a constructed Hindi-Chinese parallel sentence corpus and the CCAligned web document-level parallel corpus. Experimental results demonstrate the exceptional performance of the constructed parallel sentence alignment model, enabling efficient and reliable extraction of bilingual parallel sentences from document-level corpora.

Title: Research on self-training-based low-resource parallel sentence pair extraction
Abstract: Parallel sentence pair extraction plays a crucial role in cross-language information processing and the construction of parallel corpora for low-resource languages. This study proposes a Siamese Network framework (PCF) combined with a co-attention mechanism, and solves the data scarcity problem in the low-resource parallel sentence pair extraction task through a double selector self-training method. The PCF framework enhances the semantic alignment ability between sentence pairs by introducing a co-attention mechanism. The double selector module further optimizes the performance of the model in a low-resource environment through the screening of high-confidence pseudo-labels and a curriculum learning strategy. Experiments are conducted on datasets such as BUCC-2017. The results show that PCF is significantly superior to traditional models in terms of accuracy, recall, and F1 value, providing reliable support for machine translation and cross-language information processing under low-resource conditions.

Title: Terminology Extraction Based on Document-Level Context and Domain Adaptation
Abstract: Automatic terminology extraction holds significant application value in natural language processing tasks, particularly in domain-specific knowledge graph construction, information retrieval, and machine translation. However, existing terminology extraction methods demonstrate limited performance in cross-domain scenarios due to substantial variations in linguistic conventions, term distributions, and contextual dependencies across different domain-specific texts. This paper proposes a novel terminology extraction model that integrates document-level contextual features with domain adaptation techniques. The model achieves effective alignment between source and target domain distributions through cross-sentence dependency analysis and reverse Kullback-Leibler divergence optimization, thereby enhancing generalization capabilities. Experimental results demonstrate that: (1) Document-level contextual features yield an average 3.74% improvement in F1-score; (2) The domain adaptation mechanism provides additional 2.32% F1-score enhancement, particularly improving model adaptability in low-resource target domains. Our methodology offers new perspectives for applying terminology extraction in multi-domain scenarios.

Title: Multilingual Video Translation and Speech Synthesis: A Deep Learning Approach for Seamless Language Adaptation
Abstract: This paper introduces an efficient a n d scalable pipeline for multilingual video translation, incorporating state-of-the-art modules for audio extraction, automatic speech recognition (ASR), machine translation, text-to-speech (TTS), and lip synchronization. The system directly translates video content across multiple languages, leveraging FFmpeg for audio processing, OpenAI’s Whisper model for robust ASR, and MarianMT models fine-tuned o n t he O PUS100 dataset for high-quality multilingual translations. Additionally, gTTS provides natural speech synthesis using Google’s Text-to-Speech API, while Wav2Lip precisely aligns lip movements with synthesized speech, delivering realistic video outputs. The approach has been proven successful for both high and medium-resource languages and forms a complete solution for video translation in any language. Future work will focus on extending support for low-resource languages and improving the capability of real-time processing.

Title: “Shabda Anveshak”: Comparative Review and Analysis of Marathi Part of Speech Tagging Approaches
Abstract: In Natural Language Processing (NLP), Part-of-Speech (POS) tagging is an essential task wherein each word in a sentence is assigned a grammatical category, such as noun, verb, or adjective. It enables applications such as information retrieval, text summarization, and machine translation. POS tagging poses special difficulties for Low Resource Languages like Marathi because of complicated morphology. This is addressed by a variety of techniques, such as rule-based techniques that rely on linguistic rules, and statistical models such as Hidden Markov Models (HMMs) using probabilities dependent on big annotated datasets. Hybrid models are the combination of these two approaches showing enhanced robustness. Despite their potential, machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) approaches encounter challenges because of insufficient data. This review compares recent studies and highlights the significant and emerging directions for further improving POS Taggers for Marathi.

Abstract: Tamil language processing in NLP has yet to be outstanding, mainly because of the absence of high-quality resources. In this project, a novel approach to address these limitations is to build an encoder-decoder transformer model specifically for the Tamil language. The comprehensive Tamil text dataset is augmented along with transformer architectures to further enhance the performance on tasks such as machine translation, text summarization, and generation. Using the Transformer model for processing the Tamil language holds potential for filling an important gap for underrepresented languages in NLP, and further contributes to developing more inclusive AI.

Title: Research on Speech Alignment Algorithms for Big Data-Driven Online Translation Platforms
Abstract: With the acceleration of globalization, real-time speech translation has become a core requirement for cross-language interaction. As a key module, speech alignment's accuracy directly impacts system performance. To address the limitations of existing methods in noisy environments, low-resource languages, and real-time performance, this paper proposes a speech alignment algorithm that integrates multi-scale feature extraction with a dynamic attention mechanism (MSAM-BDA). This algorithm captures different time-frequency features through multi-resolution convolution, combines dynamic attention with adaptive feature weighting, and employs a cross-lingual transfer loss to improve adaptability to low-resource languages. Experimental validation on a 1000-hour multilingual corpus (MSPC) demonstrates that the MSAM-BDA achieves an alignment error rate (AER) of 3.21 %, a 5.31 percentage point reduction compared to DTW and a 0.94 percentage point reduction compared to BiLSTM. The algorithm also achieves a processing speed of 3420 frames per second, with a 30-second speech latency of only 118ms, meeting real-time requirements. Even under extreme noise (SNR = -5dB), the AER remains at 5.40%, with a noise attenuation rate of 68.5%, significantly outperforming competing algorithms. This algorithm provides an efficient and robust speech alignment solution for online translation systems.

Title: SSL400 - A Comprehensive Word Level Dataset for Sinhala Sign Language Recognition
Abstract: In the context of increasing digital accessibility and the need for inclusive communication technologies, the demand for automated sign language recognition has grown significantly. However, Sinhala Sign Language (SSL), used by the Sri Lankan deaf community, remains underexplored due to the lack of labelled datasets and the challenges of developing recognition models for low-resource languages. This study addresses this gap by introducing an SSL dataset, specifically curated to support real-time recognition of 384 commonly used words in daily and work-related contexts. The methodology for dataset creation involved expert consultations, a structured data collection process, and multi-step labelling. These steps ensured the accurate labeling of video data, which can be used for machine learning tasks like gesture recognition, sentence formation, and speech translation. The proposed dataset lays the foundation for SSL recognition models that are fast, lightweight, and optimized for low-resource environments. Additionally, we explore the performance of initial recognition models using this dataset, demonstrating its applicability in real-world scenarios. The dataset and research outcomes provide valuable resources for the development of inclusive AI-driven communication tools for the Sinhala-speaking deaf community. This contribution addresses the pressing need for better technological support for underrepresented languages in the field of sign language recognition and processing.

Title: Designing a Swahili-Speaking Medical Chatbot for Oncology, Dermatology, and Otorhinolaryngology Care in Low-Resource Settings
Abstract: Access to specialized medical care in fields such as otorhinolaryngology, dermatology, and oncology remains critically limited in low-resource settings, particularly among Swahili-speaking populations in East Africa. This paper presents Lueji, a Swahili-speaking medical chatbot designed to assist in providing accessible health information in these domains. A major challenge in building such systems lies in the scarcity of domain-specific Swahili-language medical corpora. To address this, we constructed a Swahili dataset by automatically translating the Huatuo-26M Chinese medical corpus using the GPT-4o-mini model, followed by dataset cleaning, normalization, and human validation. The translated dataset was used to fine-tune the UlizaLlama model, resulting in a specialized chatbot capable of generating medically relevant responses in Swahili. Evaluation using BLEU, ROUGE, and GLEU metrics demonstrated significant performance gains over a baseline model, with Lueji achieving BLEU-1 of 22.17, ROUGE-1 of 31.68, and GLEU of 10.77. These results highlight the effectiveness of combining automatic translation with supervised fine-tuning for low-resource language adaptation. Future work will focus on expanding the dataset, incorporating real-time retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), and conducting field testing with healthcare professionals and patients.

Title: Distinguishing Between Saint(Sadhu) and Common(Cholit): A Bangla BERT Approach to Bengali Language Classification
Abstract: Bengali is the fifth most spoken language in the world. It displays diglossia in two different registers: formal/classical Sadhu Bhasha and modern/colloquial Cholit Bhasha. Because of their clear grammatical, lexical, and stylistic distinctions, it is still very difficult to distinguish these registers computationally. In order to solve the major difficulties in processing a morphologically complex and historically varied language, this research suggests an automated method for dividing Bengali sentences into Sadhu and Cholit kinds. We use both sophisticated deep learning techniques and automated machine learning (PyCaret). The BanglaBERT model performed better than the others, achieving 95.09% accuracy with AUC(0.9703). The organizing of digital libraries, educational technology, the preservation of cultural heritage, and several Bengali NLP applications like machine translation and sentiment analysis can all benefit from accurate register categorization. By combining cutting-edge computational methods with conventional linguistic insights, this research advances NLP capabilities for low-resource languages.

Abstract: The development of Large Language Models (LLMs) for underrepresented languages is challenged by the lack of large-scale, high-quality datasets. This paper addresses this limitation by leveraging transfer learning and zero-shot learning to develop robust models for low-resource languages. Using pre-trained LLMs such as GPT-4, we fine-tuned the models on datasets containing as few as 5,000 samples. The resulting models achieved notable improvements: translation accuracy with BLEU scores up to 49.8, task-specific F1 scores reaching 0.74, and perplexity values reduced to 17.5 with larger datasets of 20,000 samples. Zero-shot evaluations further demonstrated strong generalization capabilities, with F1 scores of 0.68 in Zulu sentiment analysis, 0.67 in Pashto named entity recognition, and 0.62 in Amharic machine translation. These findings highlight an effective, scalable approach to language modeling in data-constrained environments. Our work underscores the value of repurposing multilingual LLMs to create inclusive NLP technologies that bridge the language divide and support underrepresented linguistic communities.

Title: Performance of Transformer-Based Models in Dholuo-Swahili Translation for Low-Resourced Language
Abstract: This study evaluates the performance of three transformer-based models: OpenNMT-py, BERT, and LLaMA 3.2 3B in translating Dholuo to Swahili, with a focus on the challenges faced in low-resource language translation. Although Swahili is widely supported in translation systems, Dholuo remains largely underrepresented. Using parallel corpora from KenCorpus and THiNK, we applied data augmentation techniques to enrich the dataset before training the models. Evaluation using BLEU, METEOR, ChrF++, and COMET metrics showed that OpenNMT-py achieved the highest performance, with a BLEU score of 41.77%, METEOR of 48.71%, ChrF++ of 64.46%, and COMET of 75.24%. In contrast, BERT and LLaMA 3.2 3B yielded significantly lower scores across all metrics. These results highlight the effectiveness of task-specific models in low-resource machine translation. Future work will explore the use of additional parallel corpora, and multilingual transfer learning to further improve performance and support wider coverage of low-resourced African languages.

Title: Automatic Post-Editing (APE) Algorithm for Machine Translation Based on Deep Learning
Abstract: Existing automatic post-editing (APE) technologies still face significant shortcomings in handling complex contextual relationships, integrating multi-source input information, and fine-tuning generated content. This paper introduces multiple post-editing modeling strategies within a deep learning framework and systematically constructs three representative models: a Bi-RNN+Attention architecture, a multi-input Transformer architecture, and a generative pre-trained language model (GPT-style). In the experimental design, this paper examines the impact of different architectures on translation error detection, contextual consistency capture, and low-resource transfer capabilities. Results show that when the model receives both SRC and MT as input, its TER (Translation Editing Rate) reaches a minimum of 21.3, with BLEU (Bilingual Evaluation Understudy) and ChrF++ (Character n-gram F-score Plus Plus) scores of 71.9 and 77.8, respectively, significantly outperforming any single-input configuration. This demonstrates that dual-source information fusion can effectively enhance semantic integrity, structural alignment, and linguistic naturalness.

Title: Maneno Yetu: Dynamic Corpus Construction and Pretraining for Swahili NLP
Abstract: Swahili occupies a central place in African linguistic landscapes, yet it is significantly under-resourced in NLP, reflecting a mismatch between speaker population and data availability. We introduce Maneno Yetu, a dynamic and extensible corpus designed to address this gap. It is continuously updated with diverse sources such as news articles, blogs, literature, and educational content. This structure enables robust pretraining and fine-tuning for Swahili NLP. The evolving nature of the corpus allows for longitudinal linguistic analysis, providing a unique opportunity to track language change over time. It also serves as a foundation for creating niche, task-specific datasets in low-resource settings. Building on Maneno Yetu, we present the Swahili Language Foundational Model (SLFM), a transformer-based model trained to support core NLP tasks including tokenization, part-of-speech tagging, machine translation, and abusive language detection. Both the corpus and model are released publicly to support reproducible research and foster community-driven development in African language technologies.

Title: Evaluating Large Language Models for Pronoun Resolution in Punjabi: A Comparative Study of ChatGPT and Gemini
Abstract: In artificial intelligence, Large Language Models (LLMs) are becoming essential, especially in Natural Language Processing (NLP). These models enable researchers to develop more complex and effective solutions for various NLP tasks, including text summarization, sentiment analysis, question-answering systems, and many more. Reference resolution (pronoun resolution), is essential for the functionality of systems such as question-answering platforms and machine translation tools. While LLMs have demonstrated remarkable performance in reference resolution for languages with abundant resources, such as English, their effectiveness in languages with limited resources remains unknown. This paper evaluates LLMs, specifically ChatGPT and Gemini, emphasizing their ability to resolve references in Punjabi, a resource-poor language. In addition to assessing the current capabilities of these models, our research aims to identify their shortcomings and areas for improvement. The experiment indicates that ChatGPT demonstrates superior performance compared to Gemini, but additional refinement and enhancement are needed to produce more consistent and reliable outcomes.

Title: Impact of Translation on Sentiment Analysis of Bengali Rumor Texts: A Multi-Criteria Approach
Abstract: Sentiment analysis of public perceptions on social media and digital platforms has grown significantly in recent years. While natural language processing (NLP) has advanced for resource-rich languages (e.g., English, Chinese), applying sentiment analysis to low-resource languages like Bengali remains challenging. The impact of translation quality on polarity detection (positive, negative, neutral), especially for Bengali, the fifth most spoken Indo-European language has not been thoroughly studied. This study proposes an integrated framework to analyze how translation affects polarity detection in Bengali rumor texts from Facebook. We collect rumor posts from Rumor Scanner, a fact-checking platform, along with their corresponding Facebook comments. To evaluate the translation's role, we compare machine translation (Google Translate) and manual translation in combination with lexiconbased tools (VADER, TextBlob) and a transformer-based model (BanglaBERT). Performance is assessed using accuracy, F1-score, translation quality, and processing time, with multicriteria decision-making (MCDM) techniques applied for comparative analysis. Results show that manual translation significantly outperforms automated methods in preserving sentiment polarity, providing key insights for low-resource language processing.

Title: Fact Checking in Low Resource Languages: Creating Translation-Based Datasets and Benchmarking for Farsi
Abstract: Misinformation poses significant risks to public health, trust, and social cohesion. However, fact-checking datasets and models remain scarce in low-resource languages (LRLs) such as Amharic, Burmese, Chechen, Farsi (Persian), Maguindanao, Pashto, and Uighur. Creating large, manually curated datasets in these languages is often prohibitively expensive. This paper proposes a resource-efficient method for building fact-checking datasets in LRLs using machine translation. Specifically, we introduce FNC-1F, a Farsi dataset created by translating the widely used Fake News Challenge dataset (FNC-1) from English to Farsi with the No Language Left Behind model. Using FNC-1F, we fine-tuned and evaluated three transformer-based models ParsBERT-FA, RoBERTa-fa-ZWNJ, and mDeBERTa-v3. We also validated their performance on real-world, manually curated Farsi test data. Results show that models trained on the translated dataset generalize effectively to native Farsi with only minor performance loss. Beyond presenting a practical approach for building fact-checking datasets in LRLs, this work also establishes the first benchmark for evidence-based fact-checking in Farsi.

Title: ThaiMRC: A Comprehensive Corpus for Advancing Machine Reading Comprehension in Thai
Abstract: Existing corpora for many low-resource languages often suffer from a lack of diversity and lack natural linguistic flow. While some efforts have attempted to address these limitations by leveraging machine translation or synthesis with generative AI, the results are often suboptimal. This paper introduces ThaiMRC, a new, human-created corpus for Thai Machine Reading Comprehension. We developed the corpus based on three core principles: diversity, naturalness, and accuracy. A key innovation in our approach is the use of the Data, Information, Knowledge, and Wisdom (DIKW) framework, which helps generate deep and complex question-answer pairs. Our quality assessment process involved three state-of-the-art LLMs as judges alongside human linguists. The corpus was used in the AI Thailand Benchmark 2025 competition, where models fine-tuned on the ThaiMRC corpus outperformed a baseline method that relied solely on one-shot prompting. We share methodology, experimental results, and findings, aiming to guide the creation of high-quality corpora for low-resource languages further.

Title: Cross-Lingual Transfer Learning for Low-Resource Language Sentiment Analysis
Abstract: Sentiment analysis in low-resource languages remains challenging due to limited annotated data and linguistic resources. This study leverages cross-lingual transfer learning using multilingual pre-trained model of mBERT to transfer sentiment-related knowledge from high-resource languages. To enhance performance, a similarity graph-based approach is introduced that computes semantic and structural similarities between language embeddings, where the graph's edge weights determine the degree of similarity between low-resource and high-resource languages. These weights dynamically adjust the transfer learning strategy, prioritizing classification models from more relevant high resource languages for respective low resource languages. Translating low-resource languages helps improve performance, but it may introduce translation biases that affect downstream tasks. To address this gap, this work employs multiple machine translation (MT) models such as Google Trans late, NLLB, MBart50 and M2M100 to translate languages and apply ensemble methods to select the most consistent translation among multiple outputs. This graphenhanced learning framework demonstrates significant improvements in sentiment analysis and provides a scalable, adaptive solution for low resource languages.

Title: Fine-Tuning and Model Size Effects on NLLB-Based Minangkabau-Indonesian Translation: A Comparative Analysis
Abstract: Minangkabau, one of Indonesia’s many regional languages, faces digital underrepresentation and endangerment. Advances in machine translation, particularly using multilingual models like No Language Left Behind (NLLB), present an opportunity to preserve such low-resource languages through effective translation systems. This study investigates and compares the impact of fine-tuning three NLLB model variants: distilled 600M, distilled 1.3B, and full 3.3B, on bidirectional Minangkabau-Indonesian translation tasks. Using a 10,969-sentence parallel corpus, each model is fine-tuned under consistent hyperparameters. Performance is evaluated using sacreBLEU and chrF++ metrics. Fine-tuning led to significant improvements across all model sizes. The 3.3B model achieved the best results in the Minangkabau–Indonesian direction, with a sacreBLEU of 59.80 and chrF++ of 76.97. In the reverse direction, the 1.3B model performed best, with a sacreBLEU of 55.53 and chrF++ of 74.58. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of fine-tuning multilingual models for low-resource language pairs. Additionally, larger model sizes generally yielded better performance, though the observed improvements at larger scales were relatively modest in this setting.

Title: Improving Translation Accuracy Through Advanced Language Detection
Abstract: Effective language identification (LID) is crucial for robust multilingual machine translation (MT), yet current approaches face a critical trade-off between accuracy and efficiency. While static LID methods lack adaptability, joint LID-MT systems introduce computational overhead that limits scalability. This paper presents a novel dynamic LID framework that addresses these challenges by adjusting language representations in real time during translation. Our lightweight module improves MT accuracy while maintaining low latency, particularly benefiting low-resource languages and noisy text scenarios.Experimental results demonstrate significant gains over existing approaches, with +3.5 BLEU improvement for high-resource languages and +6.2 BLEU for low-resource languages, while adding only 8.3% latency overhead a substantial improvement over prior work. The system also achieves 97.5% LID accuracy, outperforming static and joint training baselines. These advances make multilingual MT more practical for real-world applications, where input quality and language variability pose persistent challenges.By integrating dynamic LID with minimal computational cost, this work bridges an important gap between theoretical language representation research and deployable MT systems. The proposed approach opens new directions for adaptive, efficient, and inclusive multilingual translation technologies.

Title: A Bibliometric Analysis of Embedding Techniques for Addressing Meaning Conflation Deficiency in Low-Resourced Languages
Abstract: Meaning Conflation Deficiency (MCD): the phenomenon whereby a singular vector representation amalgamates many meanings of a word—continues to pose a significant difficulty in Natural Language Processing, especially for morphologically complex and low-resourced languages. This shortcoming obstructs precise semantic comprehension, particularly in activities such as word meaning disambiguation and machine translation. This study performs a bibliometric analysis of academic research from 2014 to 2025 focused on embedding strategies aimed at addressing MCD. Using data sourced from Scopus and Web of Science and visualised via VOSviewer, the research delineates significant publishing patterns, identifies prominent authors and journals, and explores topic progression within embedding paradigms. Findings indicate a distinct evolution from static embeddings (e.g., Word2Vec, GloVe) to advanced context-aware and multi-sense models like ELMo, BERT, and multilingual transformers. The results highlight an increasing interest in graph-based and hybrid embeddings specifically designed for the linguistic intricacies of low-resourced languages. This work serves as a thorough reference for future research focused on creating more effective embedding techniques to alleviate meaning conflation in various linguistic contexts.

Title: Effective Pivot Language Strategies for Low-Resource Translation via Prompting Large Language Models
Abstract: Traditional fine-tuning methods for low-resource machine translation, while effective in enhancing translation quality, are often constrained by substantial computational and data requirements, limiting their practical utility. Prompt tuning large language models (LLMs) has recently emerged as a lightweight alternative, activating latent knowledge through carefully crafted prompts without altering model parameters. However, existing prompting strategies often struggle with semantic misalignment, particularly when translating between distant low-resource language pairs. In this paper, we investigate the efficacy of incorporating a pivot language strategy to address this “understanding misalignment”. Building upon the DUAT-I prompting framework, we propose two distinct pivot-based approaches using English as the interlingua: (1) a sentence-level two-stage translation pathway and (2) a wordlevel pathway focusing on granular lexical mapping. Extensive experiments on six low-resource language pairs from the FLORES-200 benchmark, utilizing prominent LLMs and evaluated with COMET, demonstrate that our pivot strategies, especially the sentence-level approach, significantly outperform direct translation and few-shot prompting baselines.

Title: Natural Language Processing for Multilingual and Low-Resource Languages
Abstract: Multilingual and low-resource NLP is a challenging task as it suffers from the lack of labelled data, high annotation cost, and the paucity of language-specific resources. We present an integrated framework that uses pre-trained multilingual encoders, synthetic data augmentation, active learning, and cross-lingual transfer to enhance performance on foundational NLP tasks, including part-of-speech tagging, named entity recognition, and machine translation. We use XLM-Roberta as a multilingual encoding layer and transfer learn per-task on four low resource languages: Amharic, Guarani, Uyghur, and Yoruba. We experimented with data augmentation via back-translation and paraphrasing, which greatly improved training corpus, and active learning, which reduced manual annotation by up to 40%. Cross-lingual transfer from related languages also improved system performance for which over and above language-specific baselines, improved F1-scores in the range of 8–10% were recorded. Experiments on low-resource benchmarks corroborate the effectiveness of the framework, with BLEU score improvements in up to 10 points and stable convergence gains. The proposed approach provides a scalable and cost-effective mechanism to improve the performance of NLP for low-resource languages.

Title: Mitigating Local Language Loss through Dictionary-Based Translator Design Using Corpus Approach
Abstract: Many regional languages in Indonesia are at risk of extinction due to limited digital resources. Most research in machine translation focuses on major languages, leaving regional low-resource languages underrepresented. This study proposes a conceptual design of a translator that integrates dictionary-based and corpus-based approaches. Using a descriptive-qualitative method through literature review, it analyzes prior works on bilingual dictionaries, corpora, and hybrid translation systems. The proposed design consists of three components: a bilingual dictionary to provide word equivalents, a corpus to capture contextual meaning, and data augmentation techniques such as paraphrasing and back-translation to expand limited datasets. The expected result is a translation model that achieves better performance than using only dictionary or corpus approaches. Dictionary-based methods handle basic vocabulary but often lose contextual meaning, while corpus-based methods help interpret idioms, cultural nuances, and polysemy. Evaluation metrics such as BLEU, METEOR, and TER will measure translation quality. This research contributes a framework for developing effective translation systems for regional languages with limited data and aims to implement it as a user-friendly, web-based application accessible to the public.

Title: Performance and Efficiency Trade-offs in Transformer Models for Kannada Sentiment Analysis
Abstract: Sentiment analysis in resource-scarce languages like Kannada is difficult because of lack of labeled data and the complex linguistic characteristics of Dravidian languages. A machine translation tool is used to create the labeled dataset in Kannada from a high resource language English. The created dataset is analyzed by finetuning Transformer models like MuRIL, IndicBERT, mBERT, XLM-RoBERTa(XLM-R), and DistilBERT, for sentiment classification in Kannada. The sentiments are classified into three classes: positive, negative, and neutral. We analyze the performance of these models on native-script Kannada text, highlighting the advantages of language-specific pre-training in MuRIL and the efficiency of IndicBERT in resource-constrained settings. Our experiments reveal that MuRIL and XLM-R outperform other models in capturing the intricate syntactic and semantic features of Kannada. Additionally, we discuss the trade-offs between performance and computational efficiency, with DistilBERT and IndicBERT offering a viable option for real-time applications. The results demonstrate the critical role of tailored pre-training and fine-tuning strategies for low-resource sentiment analysis, paving way for improved natural language understanding in Kannada and other Dravidian languages.
