Title: Development of End2End automatic speech recognition system using Wav2Vec2.0 for Punjabi language
Abstract: Humans communicate through speech, which is a primary and natural source of communication. A human-computer interface based on speech recognition is one of the next-generation technologies. Automatic speech recognition (ASR) involves converting speech into words using a computer program, the development of which remains a challenging task because of its interdisciplinary nature. Further, the development of ASR requires huge amount of speech data (corpus), the collection and annotation of which is a prime and very important task and requires careful consideration as it is very time consuming. This article elaborates speech recognition systems, their classification, applications, working, and factors affecting ASR, accompanied by most important process of ASR development i.e. corpus collection, its prerequisites and parameters that need to be considered while planning corpus collection. Further, the article focuses on designing state-of-the-art End-to-End (E2E) system using Facebook`s speech recognition model Wav2Vec2.0, for the Punjabi language, which is considered as a low resource language. The Wav2Vec2.0 model gives 37 % WER on test set. The developed E2E system for Punjabi language has wide range of prospective applications in several fields such as education, machine translation, healthcare and customer services.

Title: Fine-Tuning a Machine Learning Model to Detect Covid-19 Misinformation in Xitsonga
Abstract: This paper explores the effectiveness of models, specifically Multilingual Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (mBERT) and Random Forest, for detecting misinformation about Coronavirus Disease 2019 (COVID-19) in Xitsonga, a South African language. The focus is on evaluating how synonym replacement and translation techniques can enhance model performance for misinformation detection by comparing the mBERT and Random Forest models in terms of accuracy, precision, recall, and F1 score. The continuous spread of misinformation during the pandemic COVID-19 has highlighted the need for accurate and efficient classification systems, especially in low-resource languages. To address this challenge, we enhanced an English news dataset using two data augmentation techniques: synonym replacement and translation into Xitsonga using the Marian Machine Translation (MarianMT) model. We fine-tuned mBERT for sequence classification and compare its performance with Random Forest classification model using Term Frequency-Inverse Document Frequency (TF-IDF) features. The results demonstrate that mBERT achieves good accuracy, precision, recall, and F1 score compared to Random Forest. This paper contributes to the field of misinformation detection by introducing a multilingual approach and improving classification performance in low-resource languages.

Title: Human-AI Collaborative Design of ReActNet-XGBoost Hardware Accelerator for Personalized Wearable ECG Monitoring
Abstract: The rapid expansion of personalized healthcare has positioned wearable electrocardiogram (ECG) monitoring systems as a pivotal solution for continuous cardiac assessment. However, achieving real-time signal classification under strict power and resource constraints remains a core challenge for edge-based deployment. While convolutional neural networks (CNNs) offer excellent feature extraction capabilities, their intensive computational and memory demands impede efficient implementation on lightweight hardware platforms. To overcome these limitations, we propose a hybrid hardware accelerator integrating a binarized ReActNet backbone for low-overhead feature extraction with an XGBoost decision tree classifier that provides interpretable and hardware-efficient inference. The ReActNet module leverages binary convolution operations to reduce arithmetic complexity, while the XGBoost component replaces dense layers, enhancing model transparency and reducing logic resource usage. To further streamline deployment, we introduce a generative hardware synthesis methodology based on large language models (LLMs), enabling automatic translation of trained XGBoost models into synthesizable VHDL code from their JSON representation. This LLM-assisted workflow significantly reduces development time, eliminates manual RTL coding, and promotes modular, reusable classifier generation adaptable to evolving clinical models. The proposed system is evaluated through RTL-level simulation and synthesis targeting low-power, resource-constrained FPGA platforms, demonstrating its architectural feasibility for real-time ECG classification at the edge. These findings highlight a unified and scalable framework that fuses binary neural networks, interpretable classifiers, and generative AI techniques to accelerate hardware-software co-design and broaden the deployment of edge AI in wearable health applications.

Title: Cross-Lingual Transfer Learning for POS Tagging in Low-Resource Indian Languages: A Hindi–Dogri–Punjabi Case Study
Abstract: Part-of-Speech (POS) tagging is a fundamental task in Natural Language Processing (NLP), and the basis of another set of applications, including machine translation, question answering, and information retrieval. Most of the Indian languages, such as Dogri as low-resourced, unlike high-resource languages which benefit from large annotated corpora. The paper examines the topic of cross-lingual transfer learning in the Dogri POS tagging on Hindi and Punjabi as a source language. We compare three multilingual transformer-based models (mBERT, IndicBERT and XLM-R) in the zero-shot, few-shot, and full fine-tuning conditions. Findings indicate that with the use of few-shot learning that studies zero-shot transfer, Dogri obtains 81.5% and 88.3% accuracy using 500 annotated Dogri sentences. Full finetuning with mBERT achieves the highest accuracy of 93.1 percent, exceeding a BiLSTM-CRF supervised baseline. Experiments also indicate that multi-source transfer from Hindi and Punjabi is better than transfer between a single source transfer and also that script alignment (transliteration of Punjabi to Devanagari) improves cross-lingual performance. These results demonstrate the feasibility of developing rapid POS taggers through crosslinguistic transfer of low-resource Indian languages, particularly when based on typologically related, script-aligned source languages.

Title: A Hybrid Rule-Driven and Unsupervised Learning Framework for High-Accuracy Malayalam Stemming
Abstract: Stemming is a very important part of Natural Language Processing (NLP) operations like information retrieval, text classification, and machine translation because it minimizes the lexical variants to a shared root. The agglutinative and complex morphological Malayalam language has large patterns of suffixation that complicate the use of traditional stemmers. The paper presents a better hybrid stemming architecture that combines a suffix-stripping engine that is linguistically based with an unsupervised K-Means clustering module. The morphological component is first carried out through the rule-based component in which handcrafted suffix heuristics are used based on the Malayalam inflectional and derivational patterns. The clustered refinement phase then clusters stem candidates according to similarity of vectors, and allows word perfecting over-stemming and understemming mistakes to be automatically corrected. Benchmark Malayalam corpus experimental evaluation shows much higher accuracy, precision, and recall than current rule-based and statistical stemmers. These findings confirm the efficacy of the integration of linguistics with machine learning tools in order to achieve strong morphological normalization in low resource Indian languages. The suggested structure offers a scalable platform on behalf of sophisticated Malayalam NLP-based systems such as semantic retrieval and text analytics at scale.

Title: Post Editing English to Hindi Translation with Fine Tuned Qwen Models
Abstract: English-to-Hindi machine translation (MT) poses significant challenges due to structural, morphological, and se-mantic complexities between the two languages. This paper introduces a novel automatic post-editing (APE) framework leveraging the Qwen-3 large language model to enhance translation quality. The proposed methodology integrates three key components: (i) data augmentation through contextual synonym replacement to enrich linguistic diversity, (ii) prompt engineering tailored to encapsulate complex linguistic and semantic post-editing instructions, and (iii) parameter-efficient fine-tuning using QLoRA to adapt Qwen-3 for the APE task without excessive computational overhead. The system was evaluated on the multi-domain EnIndic dataset, consisting of MT outputs and human post-edited references. The experimental results show a significant improvement in the performance with BLEU 61.48, ChrF++ 93.87, TER 23.09, WER 1.3857, which is higher as compared to baseline results of BLEU 2.16, ChrF++ 2.49, TER 116.14, and WER 0.7311. The results highpoint the helpfulness of our outline in generating linguistically accurate and semantically reliable translations. However, there are silent limitations to generalizing the process to low-resource language pairs and defining its applicability to other datasets and domains. These questions will proposal future re-search opportunities to the NLP community, as they will provide a casual to progress more powerful multilingual post-editing systems.

Title: Design and Implementation of Mongolian Chinese English Translation System Based on AI Large Model
Abstract: Against the backdrop of deepening globalization and the rapid development of AI-driven cross-lingual communication, minority languages like traditional Mongolian face challenges in intelligent translation due to limited technological support, hindering cross-cultural exchanges. This study aims to address the intelligent translation needs between Chinese, traditional Mongolian, and English. Existing translation tools suffer from shortcomings such as inadequate semantic understanding of complex grammatical differences between Mongolian and Chinese, limited support for traditional Mongolian scripts, and inability to achieve deep trilingual mutual translation. To tackle these issues, this study designs a translation platform integrating semantic web technology and AI large models, adopting the Spring Boot framework and Thymeleaf template engine for front-end and back-end architecture, combining MySQL database for basic translation, and introducing the DeepSeek-v3 model to enhance translation modules. This method achieves accurate handling of traditional Mongolian (Unicode 14.0 compliance), supports trilingual mutual translation, and improves cultural adaptability through contextual semantic understanding. The test results show that the system’s translation accuracy exceeds 80% (with Mongolian-English mutual translation reaching 82.1 BLEU-4), and it effectively supports cross-lingual lexical semantic comparison. This research provides a feasible technical solution for low-resource language machine translation, enriches the application of AI large models in minority language processing, and contributes to advancing global multilingual intelligent communication.

Title: Assessment of Amharic-English Literary Translations Quality by Ryabko-Savina Method
Abstract: Translation quality assessment constitutes a central challenge in computational linguistics. This study investigates the application of the Ryabko–Savina (RS) method for evaluating translation accuracy. Traditional evaluation approaches, which rely on stylistic metrics and machine learning, are often influenced by text length and predefined linguistic features. To address these limitations, the RS method offers the possibility to utilize compression algorithms for translation quality analysis. The study examines the unconscious stylistic influence of translators by comparing multiple translations of the same literary works and applies the Ryabko–Savina method to differentiate between original Amharic texts, human-translated Amharic-to-English texts, and machine-translated outputs. Experiments were conducted using six original Amharic novels for authorship style analysis and well-known translated works produced by human and machine translators for translation quality assessment. Based on Cramer’s coefficient across multiple experiments, the Prediction by Partial Matching (PPM) algorithm exhibited the highest stability and was employed for subsequent analyses. The Ryabko–Savina method achieved high classification accuracy, with Cramer’s coefficients of 0.89 for Amharic authorship identification, 0.762 and 1.00 for human-translated texts, 0.91 for machine-translated Amharic-to-English texts, and 0.53 for English–Amharic machine translation tasks. Overall, the findings demonstrate that the Ryabko–Savina method provides a robust, language-independent framework for translation quality assessment, particularly advantageous for low-resource languages such as Amharic.

Title: Formality Classification in Bangla and Romanized Bangla: Ensemble Learning and Multi-Model Benchmark for Shadhu-Cholito Detection
Abstract: The explosive rise of Banglish, a Romanized version of Bangla increasingly used in informal internet communication, has blurred traditional language boundaries and presented new challenges to computational linguistics. Among the most critical but less examined is the distinction between Shadhu (formal) and Cholito (informal) registers in both Bangla and Banglish, each of which sharply differs in syntax, morphology, and style. This paper introduces the initial benchmark setup for cross-script register classification for Bangla and Banglish. The four-class dataset was formed by combining public Bangla corpora with a new curated Banglish dataset. An extensive collection of models like TF-IDF classifiers, FastText-based baselines, and multilingual transformer architectures was experimented with in isolation and employing ensemble methods. Experimental assessment shows that BanglaT5 achieved 96.34% accuracy, 0.9634 macro F1-score on Bangla, FastText + Logistic Regression performed best on Banglish (85.88% accuracy, 0.8582 macro F1-score), and Weighted Soft Voting ensemble outperformed all individual models on the combined dataset (90.79% accuracy, 0.9074 macro F1-score), establishing strong baselines for this low-resource, codemixed environment. In addition to benchmarking, the study highlights the importance of register-aware processing to downstream tasks such as sentiment analysis, machine translation, and conversational AI. Although there are still problems-primarily in handling realworld Banglish spelling variation and code-switching-the approach laid out here is a proper foundation for future Bangla NLP work.

Title: Benchmarking Bengali Dialect Identification: A Comparative Study of Machine Learning, DNN, and Transformer Architectures
Abstract: Bengali is a linguistically abundant language that is used by more than 250 million individuals living in various regions and whose dialects vary in terms of the region. The automatic detection of these dialects is important in improving natural language processing (NLP) systems including speech recognition, machine translation, and social media analysis. Regardless of this significance, the Bengali dialect recognition research is still under-investigated as quality annotated data and thorough model analysis are not common. This paper provides a benchmark study with a recently curated and balanced dialect dataset of 5 large regional dialects of Bengali: Noakhali, Sylhet, Barishal, Mymensingh and Chittagong. We test 14 models, such as conventional machine learning (ML) classifiers, deep neural networks (DNNs), transformer-based models, and hybrids. XLM-ROBERTa has the highest accuracy (94.10 %), and F1-score $(94.11 \%)$. A hybrid between XLM-R and BiLSTM, CNN, and attention can also be used with a score of 93.15% on both of these measures. In addition, we also calculate Cohen's Kappa and Matthews Correlation Coefficient (MCC) of 92.62, to confirm consistency. In comparison with the previous research work, our method does not only lead to the state-of-the-art results, but also the most comprehensive comparative assessment so far. This study establishes a solid base in the dialectal studies in Bengali and also shows the possibility of transformer and hybrid models in a low-resource environment.

Title: Empowering Language Understanding Through Advanced Language Models and NLP Innovations
Abstract: The development of Tamil Question Answering (QA) systems faces significant challenges due to the language’s low-resource status and language complexity. In this work, we specifically address these challenges by implementing multilingual contrastive training and code-switching strategies to improve model performance on Tamil QA tasks. Code switching-where speakers alternate between two or more languages within a conversation or sentence. In our approach, code-switching is applied primarily in two ways: as a data augmentation technique and to better handle real-world two language Tamil-English QA scenarios. Leveraging powerful models like LLMs, Transformers, and BERT can greatly enhance Tamil language processing, enabling applications such as machine translation, subtitle generation. A critical part of our approach involves assembling and utilizing carefully curated datasets, including Parallel corpora that map Tamil to other languages, high-quality transcribed speech data, and digitized obtained through OCR pipelines form the backbone for such efforts. These datasets form the foundation for model training and evaluation. Beyond the data itself, Tamil’s rich morphology—with words carrying multiple layers of grammatical meaning—and its broad spectrum of dialects, from formal centami to regional colloquial varieties, complicate model development. To address these hurdles, researchers increasingly turn to cross-lingual transfer learning, synthetic data generation, and semi-supervised approaches to improve model generalization despite limited native-language resources. This work explores these challenges and opportunities, focusing on sourcing datasets, leveraging existing models, and applying effective techniques to develop a reliable Tamil QA system.

Title: Large Language Models in Multilingual and Low-Resource Language Contexts
Abstract: Thus, there are great potential advantages of the constant development of new artificial intelligence (AI) technologies to save and, subsequently, reconstruct endangered indigenous languages, many of which are now threatened by extinction due to globalization and the prevalence of the major world languages. New approaches for documentation, translation, and education in spoken and written languages can be applied by using AI-based tools, language models, and machine translation systems to help document and translate these languages. Nonetheless, potential problems of applying AI to language documentation are just as important, such as ownership, data privacy, cultural and social bias, and possibilities of exploitation. In this paper, we investigate the potential risks and management issues related to the deployment of artificial intelligence in archiving threatened indigenous languages. We explore the use of VGG11 and VGG16, which are primarily image recognition models typically used for tasks such as visual data analysis, including the recognition of handwritten texts in endangered languages. While VGG11 and VGG16 are leveraged in this context for analyzing visual data, the focus is on AI's broader contribution to language documentation and preservation. We also examine both the potential benefits and risks of AI for indigenous languages, particularly emphasizing the importance of community-driven strategies. Ensuring inclusive benefits, honoring regional traditions, and establishing accountable management frameworks for AI implementation are crucial issues. To support linguistic diversity, this article advocates for a balanced approach to AI in language preservation, emphasizing sustainable models and ethical governance.

Abstract: With the advent of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GAI) and Large Language Models (LLM), new flavour of teaching by replacing the humans has emerged in the recent educational scenarios. In this context, this research article aims to develop the hybrid generative AI framework that utilizes finetuned language model by the meta-heuristic technique to achieve the high translation accuracy. The suggested hybrid framework incorporates the fine-tuned Mistral-7B model integrated with the meta-heuristic algorithm for a achieving the high rate of translated contents in accordance to the student's known language. The comprehensive experimentation is carried out using the different multi-lingual datasets and various metrics such as BLEU, ChF and WER are analysed and validated with the other language models such as LLAMA, GEMMA, GPT.3.0 and BERT. The complete data -driven outcomes demonstrated that the proposed meta-heuristic model has achieved BLEU score of 0.9, chF score of 0.99 and WER with 0.01, which outshines the other models in producing the enhanced reliability of produced contents. These findings highlights the potential of hybrid large language models for generating the more reliable contents, offering the more scalable system for breaking the language barrier

Title: A Comparative Study: Leveraging BERT and K-fold Cross Validation for UPOS Tagging in Bengali
Abstract: Universal Dependency (UD) infrastructure-based Part-of-Speech tagging also called UPOS tagging, holds critical importance for the development of higher-level Natural Language Processing (NLP) applications in Bengali. Due to its limited resources and lack of exploration, this study represents a manually created Bengali UPOS dataset and a comparative analysis utilizing recurrent-based deep learning models and transformer-based techniques to enhance tagging reliability. For the creation of the dataset, the information was gathered from news, tales, Wikipedia, and various subject areas in order to preserve the Bengali language’s prevalence, and we have painstakingly compiled over 2200 sentences with more than 32000 tokens into a treebank. In order to increase UPOS tagging accuracy, we adopt a transformer-based technique with multilingual BERT (mBERT) for our dataset and initially yield an 84% accuracy after fine-tuning it. Our BERT model shows a significant performance gain when k-fold cross-validation (k=5) is applied, and the accuracy dramatically improves to 92.65% on average. We also compare our approach against other recurrent-based models (e.g., LSTM, BiLSTM) that are also applied to the same dataset, and the efficacy of a transformer-based model named BERT for morphologically rich and low-resource languages like Bengali is demonstrated. The enhanced accuracy and vast dataset in Bengali UPOS tagging could significantly impact NLP applications like dependency parsing, grammar checkers, and machine translation enhancement.

Title: Memory-Optimized Offloading: Enabling LLM Fine-Tuning on Memory-Constrained Hardware
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have revolutionized natural language processing, enabling breakthroughs in applications ranging from machine translation to conversational artificial intelligence. However, fine-tuning these massive models presents significant memory challenges, especially when fine-tuning with mixed precision (FP16/FP32) to maintain efficiency and accuracy. Although existing techniques, such as the DeepSpeed fine-tuning framework, can reduce the overhead of host memory using group fine-tuning, these methods suffer from inefficient overflow detection and redundant gradient storage, greatly increasing memory requirements. These drawbacks limit the fine-tuning of large models on memory-constrained devices. To address these challenges, this paper proposes an instant gradient offloading strategy, a fine-tuning approach that significantly reduces memory overhead while maintaining fine-tuning accuracy and speed. Our solution introduces three key innovations: (1) On-the-fly overflow detection: calculated gradients are checked immediately instead of batch checking, eliminating peak memory spikes; (2) Instant gradient offloading: the gradient is offloaded to SSD and loaded when needed, minimizing CPU memory usage; (3) FP16-centric gradient offloading: the type conversion operation of the gradient data is delayed so that it uses FP16 format for data exchange with SSD. Experiments show that the proposed design reduces memory consumption by 77.8% − 85.3% compared to the DeepSpeed offload baseline while maintaining a comparable fine-tuning speed. Specifically, the proposed system can use 128GB of CPU memory to fine-tune a 98B parameter model. These advances make large-scale LLM fine-tuning possible on resource-constrained hardware.
